sections.content: Network Security, HTTPS and TLS, Digital Certificates, Hash Functions, Authentication, Data Privacy, Blockchain, Quantum Computing.

title: Malware
description: An introduction to malware, including its definition, major types such as viruses, worms, trojans, and ransomware, how infections happen, a real example, and ways to prevent and respond to it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Malware, short for malicious software, is any program that is designed to harm a computer, steal information, or give an attacker unauthorized control of a system. Malware can damage files, spy on users, lock data, or use a computer to attack others.

sections.title: History
sections.content: In 1982, a program called Elk Cloner spread between Apple II computers on floppy disks and is often named as one of the first viruses to spread outside a laboratory. In 1988, the Morris worm spread across the early Internet and slowed down thousands of computers. In 2000, the ILOVEYOU worm spread by email and affected millions of computers. In 2017, the WannaCry ransomware attack locked computers in many countries, including hospitals, and demanded payment.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Payload: The harmful action that the malware carries out, such as deleting files or encrypting data.

2. Infection Vector: The way malware reaches a system, such as an email attachment, a download, or a USB drive.

3. Vulnerability: A weakness in software that malware can use to get in.

4. Exploit: A piece of code that takes advantage of a vulnerability.

5. Antivirus Software: A program that scans for and removes known malware.

6. Signature and Behavior Detection: Antivirus tools can recognize known malware by its signature, and can also watch for suspicious behavior.

7. Patch: A software update that fixes a vulnerability.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: Malware usually reaches a computer when a user opens an infected file, clicks a harmful link, or installs a program from an untrusted source, or when it exploits an unpatched vulnerability. Once it runs, it can copy itself, hide, and carry out its payload. Some malware contacts an attacker's server to receive commands or to send stolen data. Other malware spreads automatically to other computers on the same network without any user action.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
Common types of malware include:

1. Virus: Attaches itself to a legitimate file or program and spreads when that file is shared or run.

2. Worm: Spreads by itself across networks without needing a host file.

3. Trojan: Pretends to be a useful program but performs harmful actions once installed.

4. Ransomware: Locks or encrypts a victim's files and demands payment to restore them.

5. Spyware: Secretly collects information about the user. A keylogger is spyware that records what is typed.

6. Adware: Shows unwanted advertisements, and may track browsing.

7. Rootkit: Hides malware and gives an attacker deep access to the system.

8. Botnet: A network of infected computers that an attacker controls remotely.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
Example: A ransomware attack on a small office.

1. An employee receives an email that looks like an invoice and opens the attached file.
2. The file installs ransomware, which encrypts the documents on the computer and on shared drives.
3. A message appears demanding payment to unlock the files.
4. The office can recover without paying only if it has clean backups that the malware could not reach.

How to defend:
- Keep regular backups, and store at least one copy offline.
- Install software updates and security patches promptly.
- Do not open unexpected attachments or links.
- Use antivirus software and limit user permissions.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content:
Studying malware helps in several areas:

1. Antivirus Development: Companies analyze malware to create detection rules.

2. Incident Response: Security teams investigate infections and remove them.

3. Security Awareness Training: Users learn how infections happen.

4. Digital Forensics: Investigators trace what an attacker did.

5. Network Defense: Firewalls and email filters block known threats.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: Understanding malware helps organizations and individuals prevent infections, detect them earlier, and recover faster. Knowing how it spreads makes simple habits such as updating software and backing up data much more convincing.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: No protection is perfect. New malware can avoid detection until its signature is known, and attackers often use social engineering to trick users. Antivirus software can slow a computer and may produce false alarms. Backups and updates also need continuing effort to be useful.

sections.title: Related Topics
sections.content: Network Security, Phishing, Social Engineering, Antivirus Software, Ethical Hacking, Digital Forensics, Cryptography, Incident Response.

title: Operating Systems
description: An introduction to operating systems, including their definition, main functions, key components such as the kernel and file system, common types, how they manage programs and memory, and popular examples.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: An operating system (OS) is the main system software that manages a computer's hardware and provides services for other programs. It sits between the user, the applications, and the hardware. Without an operating system, every program would have to control the keyboard, screen, memory, and storage by itself.

sections.title: History
sections.content: The earliest computers had no operating system, and operators loaded one program at a time. In the 1950s, batch systems were developed to run jobs one after another automatically. UNIX was created at Bell Labs in 1969 by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie, and many later systems were influenced by it. MS-DOS appeared in 1981, and Windows 1.0 followed in 1985. Linus Torvalds released the first version of the Linux kernel in 1991. The Apple iPhone introduced iOS in 2007, and the first Android phones were sold in 2008.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Kernel: The core of the operating system. It has full control of the hardware and provides basic services to the rest of the system.

2. Process: A program that is currently running, together with the resources it uses.

3. Thread: A smaller unit of work inside a process. A process can have several threads that run at the same time.

4. Scheduling: Deciding which process gets the CPU and for how long.

5. Memory Management: Giving each program the memory it needs and keeping programs from interfering with one another.

6. File System: The method used to name, store, and organize files on a storage device.

7. Device Driver: A small program that lets the operating system communicate with a specific piece of hardware, such as a printer.

8. User Interface: The way people use the system. A command-line interface (CLI) uses typed commands, and a graphical user interface (GUI) uses windows, icons, and menus.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: When the computer starts, a small program in firmware loads the operating system from storage into memory. The kernel then starts the system services and the user interface. When you open an application, the OS creates a process for it, gives it memory, and schedules it to use the CPU. The CPU switches between processes many times per second, so several programs seem to run at once. When a program needs a service such as reading a file, it makes a request to the kernel called a system call, and the kernel performs the task using the correct device driver.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
Operating systems can be grouped by the devices they run on:

1. Desktop and Laptop Systems: Windows, macOS, and Linux distributions such as Ubuntu.

2. Mobile Systems: Android and iOS.

3. Server Systems: Windows Server and Linux, designed to run for long periods and serve many users.

4. Embedded Systems: Small systems inside devices such as routers, TVs, and cars.

5. Real-Time Systems: Systems that must respond within a strict time limit, such as those in medical devices and industrial machines.

They can also be grouped by how they run tasks: batch systems run jobs one after another, time-sharing systems let many users share the CPU, and distributed systems spread work across several computers.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
Example: Listening to music while writing a document.

1. The OS runs two processes at once: a music player and a word processor.
2. The scheduler gives each one short turns on the CPU, switching so quickly that both seem to run at the same time.
3. The memory manager keeps each program in its own area of memory, so a crash in one does not damage the other.
4. When you press Save, the word processor asks the kernel to write the file, and the file system stores it on the drive.

You can see running processes in Windows Task Manager, or by running the command top in a Linux terminal.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content:
1. Personal Computing: Running programs and managing files on laptops and desktops.

2. Mobile Devices: Running apps and managing battery, touch input, and sensors.

3. Servers and Cloud: Hosting websites, databases, and virtual machines.

4. Embedded Devices: Controlling routers, smart TVs, and vehicles.

5. Education and Development: Learning how computers work and building software.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: An operating system lets many programs share the same hardware safely, hides hardware details from programmers, provides a consistent interface for users, and offers security features such as user accounts and file permissions.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: An operating system uses some memory and processing power itself. It can have bugs and security weaknesses, so it needs regular updates. Programs written for one operating system often cannot run on another without changes, and a failure in the kernel can crash the whole system.

sections.title: Related Topics
sections.content: Computer Hardware, File Systems, Processes and Threads, Memory Management, Linux, Windows, Android, Virtualization, Computer Architecture.

title: Binary Number System
description: An introduction to the binary number system, including place values, converting between binary and decimal, binary addition, how computers store text, and why computers use binary.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The binary number system is a way of writing numbers using only two digits, 0 and 1. It is a base-2 system, while the decimal system that people use every day is base 10. Computers use binary because their electronic circuits have two clear states, such as on and off, which map directly to 1 and 0.

sections.title: History
sections.content: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz described the modern binary number system in 1703. In 1847, George Boole published the algebra of logic, now called Boolean algebra, which works with true and false values. In 1937, Claude Shannon showed in his master's thesis that Boolean algebra could be used to design electrical switching circuits, which became the basis of digital computers. The ASCII character code, which assigns numbers to letters, was first published in 1963.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Bit: A single binary digit, either 0 or 1. The word comes from binary digit.

2. Byte: A group of 8 bits. One byte can hold 256 different values, from 0 to 255.

3. Place Value: Each position in a binary number is worth a power of 2, starting from 1 on the right, then 2, 4, 8, 16, and so on.

4. Most and Least Significant Bit: The leftmost bit has the largest value, and the rightmost bit has the smallest.

5. Hexadecimal: A base-16 system that uses the digits 0 to 9 and the letters A to F. One hexadecimal digit stands for exactly 4 bits, so it is a short way to write binary.

6. Character Encoding: A table that assigns a number to each character. ASCII and Unicode are the best known.

7. Kilobyte, Megabyte, and Gigabyte: Units of storage. In everyday use, 1 kilobyte is about 1,000 bytes, although some systems use 1,024.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: A binary number is read by adding up the place values of every position that holds a 1. For example, in 1101 the positions from the right are worth 1, 2, 4, and 8. The 1s are at the positions worth 8, 4, and 1, so the value is 8 + 4 + 1 = 13. To convert a decimal number to binary, repeatedly divide it by 2 and write down the remainders, then read the remainders from last to first. Inside the computer, all data, including numbers, text, images, and sound, is stored as patterns of bits.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
Number systems commonly used in computing:

1. Binary (base 2): Digits 0 and 1.

2. Octal (base 8): Digits 0 to 7. It was used in older systems.

3. Decimal (base 10): Digits 0 to 9.

4. Hexadecimal (base 16): Digits 0 to 9 and A to F. It is used for colors, memory addresses, and other values.

The same value written in each system: the number 255 is 11111111 in binary, 377 in octal, 255 in decimal, and FF in hexadecimal.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
Example 1: Binary to decimal.

1011 = (1 x 8) + (0 x 4) + (1 x 2) + (1 x 1) = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11

Example 2: Decimal to binary. Convert 13.

13 divided by 2 is 6 remainder 1
6 divided by 2 is 3 remainder 0
3 divided by 2 is 1 remainder 1
1 divided by 2 is 0 remainder 1

Reading the remainders from last to first gives 1101.

Example 3: Binary addition. 0101 + 0011.

The rules are 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1). Adding the two numbers gives 1000, which is 5 + 3 = 8 in decimal.

Example 4: Storing text. In ASCII, the letter A is the number 65, which is 01000001 in binary. A computer stores the word HI as the bytes for H (72) and I (73).

sections.title: Applications
sections.content:
1. Computer Memory and Storage: All data is stored as bits.

2. Networking: IP addresses and subnet masks are binary numbers written in a readable form.

3. Digital Images: Each color is stored as numbers, often written in hexadecimal, such as #FF0000 for red.

4. Programming: Bitwise operations and flags use binary values directly.

5. Digital Electronics: Logic gates and circuits work with 0 and 1.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: Binary is simple and reliable, because a circuit only needs to tell two states apart, which makes it resistant to small amounts of electrical noise. Binary arithmetic can be carried out with simple logic circuits, and it maps directly to Boolean logic.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Binary numbers are long and hard for people to read, so programmers often use hexadecimal instead. A fixed number of bits can only hold a limited range of values, and going past it causes overflow. Some decimal fractions, such as 0.1, cannot be stored exactly in binary, which leads to small rounding errors.

sections.title: Related Topics
sections.content: Hexadecimal, Boolean Algebra, Logic Gates, ASCII and Unicode, Computer Memory, IP Addressing, Data Representation, Computer Architecture.

title: HTML and CSS
description: An introduction to HTML and CSS, including how HTML structures a web page, how CSS styles it, the basic syntax of both, a working example, and how browsers combine them.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard language used to describe the structure and content of a web page, such as headings, paragraphs, images, links, and forms. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is the language used to describe how that content looks, including colors, fonts, spacing, and layout. HTML says what is on the page, and CSS says how it appears.

sections.title: History
sections.content: Tim Berners-Lee created HTML at CERN around 1989 to 1991 as part of the first World Wide Web. The first formal specification, HTML 2.0, was published in 1995, and HTML 4 followed in 1997. CSS was proposed by Hakon Wium Lie in 1994, and the first CSS recommendation was published by the W3C in 1996. HTML5 became a W3C Recommendation in October 2014 and added elements for video, audio, and page structure.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Element: A building block of an HTML page, written with a start tag, content, and an end tag, such as a paragraph element containing text.

2. Tag: The markup that marks where an element starts and ends, written between angle brackets.

3. Attribute: Extra information inside a start tag, such as the address of a link or the source of an image.

4. Semantic Elements: Elements that describe their meaning, such as header, nav, main, and footer, which help browsers and search engines understand a page.

5. Selector: The part of a CSS rule that chooses which elements to style, such as an element name, a class, or an id.

6. Property and Value: A CSS declaration has a property, such as color, and a value, such as blue.

7. Box Model: CSS treats every element as a box made of content, padding, border, and margin.

8. Cascade and Specificity: The rules that decide which style wins when several rules apply to the same element.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: When a browser receives an HTML file, it reads the tags and builds a tree of elements called the Document Object Model (DOM). It then reads the CSS and works out which rules apply to each element. Finally, it calculates the size and position of every box and paints the page on the screen. If the HTML or the CSS changes, the browser repeats these steps for the affected parts. CSS can be written in a separate file linked from the page, inside a style element, or directly in an element's style attribute, and a separate file is usually preferred because several pages can share it.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
Ways to organize and apply styles:

1. External CSS: Rules in a separate file linked to the page. This is the most common method.

2. Internal CSS: Rules written inside a style element in the page.

3. Inline CSS: Rules written in the style attribute of one element.

Common kinds of CSS selectors:

1. Element selector: Matches every element of one type, such as all paragraphs.

2. Class selector: Written with a dot, it matches every element with that class.

3. ID selector: Written with a hash sign, it matches the one element with that id.

Modern CSS layout tools include Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts and Grid for two-dimensional layouts.

sections.title: Examples
Applications
sections.content:
1. Websites: Every web page uses HTML for structure and CSS for appearance.

2. Web Applications: Interfaces for online stores, school portals, and dashboards.

3. Email Templates: Formatted emails are written in HTML.

4. Responsive Design: CSS media queries adapt a page to phones, tablets, and desktops.

5. Documentation: Many manuals and help pages are written in HTML.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: HTML and CSS are free, open standards that every browser understands. They are easy to start with, they keep content separate from design so a whole site can be restyled by changing one file, and they work on almost every device.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: HTML and CSS describe pages but cannot make decisions or process data, so JavaScript or a server-side language is needed for that. Browsers may display some CSS features differently, and large style sheets can become hard to manage without careful organization.

sections.title: Related Topics
sections.content: JavaScript, Responsive Design, DOM, Web Accessibility, Web Browsers, HTTP, CSS Frameworks, Web Development.

title: REST APIs and JSON
description: An introduction to REST APIs and the JSON format, including how clients and servers exchange data, HTTP methods and status codes, a worked example, and how Search IT uses them.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a defined way for one program to request data or actions from another. A REST API is a web API that follows the REST (Representational State Transfer) style: resources are identified by addresses, and clients use standard HTTP methods to work with them. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight text format that REST APIs commonly use to send data.

sections.title: History
sections.content: Roy Fielding described the REST architectural style in his doctoral dissertation in 2000. JSON was popularized by Douglas Crockford in the early 2000s and was based on the object notation of JavaScript. Because JSON is smaller and easier to read than XML, it replaced XML in most new web APIs during the 2010s.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Client and Server: The client, such as a browser, sends a request, and the server sends back a response.

2. Resource: A thing the API manages, such as an article or a user. Each resource has an address.

3. Endpoint: A specific address of the API, such as /api/search.

4. HTTP Method: The action requested. GET reads data, POST creates data, PUT replaces data, and DELETE removes data.

5. Status Code: A number in the response that shows the result, such as 200 for success, 404 for not found, and 500 for a server error.

6. Query Parameter: A value added to the address after a question mark, such as ?q=java.

7. Stateless: Each request contains everything the server needs, so the server does not need to remember earlier requests.

8. JSON Structure: Data is written as objects in curly braces, with name and value pairs, and as arrays in square brackets.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: The client sends an HTTP request that contains a method, an address, and sometimes extra data. The server reads the request, finds or changes the data, and sends back a response with a status code and, usually, a JSON body. The client reads the JSON and uses it, for example by showing it on the page. Because REST uses ordinary HTTP, any program that can make web requests, in any language, can use the API.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
1. REST APIs: Use standard HTTP methods and resource addresses. They are the most common style.

2. SOAP APIs: An older style that exchanges XML messages with strict rules.

3. GraphQL APIs: Let the client ask for exactly the fields it needs through one endpoint.

JSON supports these value types: string, number, true or false, null, object, and array.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
Example: The Search IT search endpoint.

Request:
GET /api/search?q=java

Response (shortened):
{
  "found": true,
  "count": 1,
  "results": [
    { "title": "Java Programming", "category": "Programming" }
  ]
}

Explanation:
- GET asks the server to read data, and q=java is the search keyword.
- found, count, and results are names, and each one has a value.
- results is an array that holds one object for each article.

In Search IT, the JavaScript in the page uses fetch() to send this request to the Java server, and the Java code builds the JSON text.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content:
1. Web and Mobile Apps: Apps load data from servers, such as posts, products, and weather.

2. Third-Party Services: Payment, map, and login services offer APIs to other developers.

3. Microservices: Large systems are split into small services that talk through APIs.

4. Configuration Files: JSON is also used to store settings and data.

5. Learning Platforms: Systems such as Search IT use an API to serve their content.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: REST APIs are simple, because they reuse standard web technology. JSON is easy for people to read and for programs to process, and almost every programming language can handle it. Clients and servers can be developed independently as long as they agree on the API.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: REST APIs can send more data than a client needs, or require several requests to collect related data. An API must be protected with authentication and input checking, or it can expose private data. JSON does not support comments or dates directly, and large responses can be slow to send.

sections.title: Related Topics
sections.content: HTTP, JavaScript, Web Servers, GraphQL, XML, Authentication, Web Security, Java Programming.

title: SQL Basics
description: An introduction to SQL, the language used to create, read, update and delete data in relational databases, with worked examples of SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY and JOIN.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for working with relational databases. A relational database stores data in tables made of rows and columns, and SQL is how you ask the database to store, find, change, or remove that data. You describe what result you want, and the database system works out the steps to produce it.

sections.title: History
sections.content: SQL grew out of Edgar F. Codd's relational model, published in 1970. In the early 1970s, Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce at IBM created a language for it, first called SEQUEL and later shortened to SQL. Oracle released the first commercially available SQL database in 1979. SQL became an ANSI standard in 1986 and an ISO standard in 1987, and it has been revised many times since. Today MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Microsoft SQL Server and Oracle Database all use SQL, each with small differences called dialects.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Table: A collection of related data arranged in rows and columns, such as a table of students.

2. Row (record): One item in a table, such as one student.

3. Column (field): One property of every row, such as name or grade. Each column has a data type, such as INT for whole numbers, VARCHAR for text, or DATE for dates.

4. Primary key: A column whose value is different for every row, so each row can be identified exactly.

5. Foreign key: A column that holds the primary key of a row in another table. It is how two tables are linked.

6. Query: A SQL statement that asks the database for data or asks it to change data.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. You write a SQL statement and send it to the database system.

2. The database checks that the statement is written correctly.

3. It plans the fastest way to find or change the data, often using indexes.

4. It runs the plan on the tables.

5. It returns the result, which is either a table of rows (for SELECT) or a message saying how many rows were changed.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
SQL commands are grouped by what they do:

1. DDL (Data Definition Language): CREATE, ALTER and DROP. They build or change the structure of tables.

2. DML (Data Manipulation Language): INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. They add, change and remove rows.

3. DQL (Data Query Language): SELECT. It reads data. Some books place SELECT under DML.

4. DCL (Data Control Language): GRANT and REVOKE. They control who may use the data.

5. TCL (Transaction Control Language): COMMIT and ROLLBACK. They save or undo a group of changes.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The examples use a table named students.

1. Create the table:
```
CREATE TABLE students (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(50),
  course VARCHAR(30),
  grade INT
);
```

2. Add a row:
```
INSERT INTO students (id, name, course, grade)
VALUES (1, 'Ana', 'BSIT', 92);
```

3. Read rows that match a condition, highest grade first:
```
SELECT name, grade FROM students
WHERE course = 'BSIT'
ORDER BY grade DESC;
```

4. Change a row:
```
UPDATE students SET grade = 95 WHERE id = 1;
```

5. Delete a row:
```
DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 1;
```

6. Count students in each course:
```
SELECT course, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY course;
```

7. Combine two tables with a JOIN:
```
SELECT students.name, enrollments.subject
FROM students
JOIN enrollments ON students.id = enrollments.student_id;
```

Always write a WHERE clause with UPDATE and DELETE. Without it, the command changes or removes every row in the table.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: SQL is used behind websites and mobile apps to store accounts, products and orders. Schools, banks and hospitals use it for their records. Businesses use it to produce reports, and data analysts use it to filter and summarize large amounts of data. Android and many desktop programs use SQLite, a small SQL database stored in a single file.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: SQL is a widely used standard, so the skill carries over between database systems. It is readable, because commands look like short English instructions. It can handle very large tables, lets many users work at the same time, and has built-in tools for security and for keeping data correct.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: SQL works best with data that fits neatly in tables, so it is less natural for loosely structured data such as documents or social graphs. Each database system has its own dialect, so some commands must be rewritten when switching systems. Poorly written queries can be slow on large tables. Queries that put user input directly into the command text are open to SQL injection, so programs must use prepared statements.

title: Database Normalization
description: An explanation of database normalization, the process of organizing tables so each fact is stored only once, with a step-by-step example that moves a messy table through First, Second and Third Normal Form.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Database normalization is the process of organizing the data in a relational database into well-structured tables so that each fact is stored in only one place. It reduces repeated data and prevents the errors that appear when repeated data is inserted, changed or deleted. The rules for how far a table has been cleaned up are called normal forms.

sections.title: History
sections.content: Edgar F. Codd introduced normalization together with the relational model. He described First Normal Form in 1970, and defined Second and Third Normal Form in 1971. In 1974, Raymond Boyce and Codd introduced a stricter version of Third Normal Form, called Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF). Later researchers added Fourth and Fifth Normal Form, which deal with rarer situations.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Redundancy: The same fact stored in many places, such as a customer phone number repeated on every order.

2. Anomalies: Problems caused by redundancy. An update anomaly means changing a fact in one row but not in the others. An insertion anomaly means being unable to record a fact until unrelated data exists. A deletion anomaly means losing a fact by deleting a row that also held other information.

3. Functional dependency: When the value of one column decides the value of another. For example, a customer id decides the customer name.

4. Primary key: The column, or group of columns, that identifies each row.

5. Normal form: A rule a table must satisfy, such as First, Second or Third Normal Form.

6. Decomposition: Splitting one table into smaller tables that are linked by keys, without losing any information.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. Look at the table and find data that repeats.

2. Decide which column, or columns, is the primary key.

3. List which columns depend on which, using functional dependencies.

4. Split the table so every column depends only on the key of its own table.

5. Link the new tables with foreign keys.

6. Check the result against each normal form, starting from the first.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
1. First Normal Form (1NF): Every cell holds a single value, there are no repeating groups of columns, and every row can be identified by a key.

2. Second Normal Form (2NF): The table is in 1NF, and every non-key column depends on the whole primary key, not on just a part of it. This matters when the key is made of more than one column.

3. Third Normal Form (3NF): The table is in 2NF, and no non-key column depends on another non-key column.

4. Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF): A stricter 3NF, in which every column that decides another column must itself be a candidate key.

5. Fourth and Fifth Normal Form: Handle special cases with multiple independent lists of values. They are rarely needed in everyday design.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
Start with one table of orders that stores everything together. The key is order_id plus product:
```
order_id | customer | phone    | product  | price
1        | Ana      | 0917-111 | Pen      | 10
1        | Ana      | 0917-111 | Notebook | 40
2        | Ben      | 0918-222 | Pen      | 10
```

Problems: Ana's phone is stored twice, and the price of a Pen is stored twice. If Ana changes her phone number, every one of her rows must be updated, or the data becomes inconsistent.

Step 1 (1NF): Each cell has one value. If an order had held the text Pen, Notebook in a single cell, we would give each item its own row, as shown above.

Step 2 (2NF): The price depends only on the product, which is just part of the key. Move it into its own table.

Step 3 (3NF): The phone depends on the customer, not on the order. Move customers into their own table.

Result:
```
customers(customer_id, name, phone)
products(product_id, product_name, price)
orders(order_id, customer_id)
order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity)
```

Now each phone number and each price is stored once, and the tables are connected by their ids.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Normalization is used when designing databases for schools, hospitals, banks, online shops and any system where records must stay correct over time. It is a standard step in database design, taught before building tables in systems such as MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: Normalized data takes less storage and is easier to keep consistent, because each fact lives in one place. Updates are simpler, and the insertion, update and deletion anomalies are avoided. The structure is clearer, which makes the database easier to understand and to change later.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Splitting data into more tables means queries must use JOINs to put it back together, which can be slower on very large reports. Going too far can make a design hard to read. For this reason, some systems, such as data warehouses, deliberately repeat data (denormalization) to read faster. Good normalization also needs careful thought about how the data really depends on itself.

title: NoSQL Databases
description: An introduction to NoSQL databases, which store data in flexible forms instead of fixed tables, covering the four main types (document, key-value, wide-column and graph), how they scale across many servers, and when to use them instead of SQL.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: NoSQL, often read as not only SQL, describes databases that store data in ways other than the fixed rows and columns of a relational database. They use flexible structures such as documents, key-value pairs or graphs, and they are designed to handle large amounts of data, fast access, and spreading the data across many servers.

sections.title: History
sections.content: The word NoSQL was first used in 1998 by Carlo Strozzi for a small relational database that did not use SQL. It became popular after 2006 and 2007, when Google published its Bigtable design and Amazon published its Dynamo design for handling huge amounts of web data. Facebook released Cassandra as open source in 2008, and MongoDB and Redis appeared in 2009. In 2009, Johan Oskarsson used the name NoSQL for a meeting about these new non-relational databases, and the name stuck.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Flexible schema: Records in the same collection do not all need the same fields, so the structure can change without rebuilding the database.

2. Horizontal scaling: Instead of buying one bigger computer (vertical scaling), more ordinary computers are added to share the work.

3. Sharding: Splitting the data into parts, called shards, and storing each part on a different server.

4. Replication: Keeping copies of the data on more than one server, so the system keeps working if one server fails.

5. CAP theorem: When a network failure splits a distributed system, it must choose between keeping the data consistent and keeping the system available. It cannot guarantee both at that moment.

6. Eventual consistency: A rule used by many NoSQL systems where all copies of the data may differ briefly but will agree after a short time. This is different from the strict ACID guarantees of traditional relational databases, although many modern NoSQL systems now offer transactions too.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. The application sends a request that uses the database's own commands or programming interface, instead of SQL.

2. The database finds which server holds the data, usually using the key or a chosen shard key.

3. It reads or writes the data on that server.

4. It copies the change to the replica servers.

5. It returns the result. Depending on the settings, it may answer after the first copy is saved, which is faster, or after several copies agree, which is safer.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
1. Document databases: Store records as JSON-like documents. Examples: MongoDB and Couchbase.

2. Key-value databases: Store each value under a unique key, like a very large dictionary. Examples: Redis and Amazon DynamoDB.

3. Wide-column databases: Store data in rows whose columns can differ, grouped into column families, which is useful for huge amounts of data. Examples: Apache Cassandra and Apache HBase.

4. Graph databases: Store items as nodes and the connections between them as relationships, which suits data about networks of people or places. Example: Neo4j.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
1. A document in a document database. Notice that the hobbies list sits inside the same record, which would need a separate table in SQL:
```
{
  "name": "Ana",
  "course": "BSIT",
  "hobbies": ["coding", "chess"]
}
```

2. Finding documents in MongoDB:
```
db.students.find({ course: 'BSIT' })
```

3. Storing and reading a value in Redis, a key-value database:
```
SET user:1 Ana
GET user:1
```

4. A graph database can answer questions such as which friends of my friends also like the same game, by following relationships instead of joining tables.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: NoSQL databases are used for social media feeds, real-time apps, online games and leaderboards, shopping carts and product catalogs, content management, and storing data from sensors. Redis is often used as a fast cache in front of another database. Graph databases are used for recommendations and for finding links between people or accounts.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: NoSQL databases can store varied data without a fixed design, and they grow by adding servers. They are very fast for the specific kinds of requests they are built for. Document databases are natural for programmers, because the stored data looks like the objects used in their code.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Most NoSQL databases do not support joins as well as SQL, so related data is often repeated, and the data must be designed around the questions the app will ask. There is no single standard query language, so skills do not transfer as easily between products. Eventual consistency can show slightly old data for a short time. For structured data with strict rules, such as bank records, a relational database is usually still the better choice.

title: Artificial Intelligence
description: An introduction to artificial intelligence (AI), covering what it is, how machines learn from data, the main types such as machine learning, deep learning and generative AI, real examples, and its benefits and risks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the field of computer science that builds systems able to do tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as recognizing images, understanding speech, translating languages, making decisions and writing text. Most modern AI does not follow a fixed list of instructions for every case. Instead, it learns patterns from large amounts of data.

sections.title: History
sections.content: In 1950, Alan Turing published a paper asking whether machines can think and proposed what is now called the Turing test. The term artificial intelligence was introduced by John McCarthy for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop, which is often seen as the start of the field. Progress later slowed during two periods of reduced funding and interest, called AI winters, in the 1970s and in the late 1980s. In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue defeated the world chess champion Garry Kasparov. Around 2012, deep learning made a major leap in image recognition, and in 2016 DeepMind's AlphaGo defeated the Go champion Lee Sedol. In 2017, researchers introduced the transformer design, which led to today's large language models and the wide use of generative AI in the 2020s.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Model: A mathematical system that takes an input, such as a photo, and produces an output, such as the word cat.

2. Machine learning: A way of building AI in which the model learns from examples instead of being given step-by-step rules.

3. Training data: The examples the model learns from. The quality and variety of this data strongly affect how good the model is.

4. Neural network: A model made of many connected layers of simple calculating units, loosely inspired by the brain.

5. Deep learning: Machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. It is behind most image, speech and language AI today.

6. Training and inference: Training is the learning stage, which needs a lot of computing power. Inference is using the trained model to answer new inputs.

7. Bias: Unfair or inaccurate results that happen when the training data is incomplete or reflects unfair patterns.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. Collect data that is related to the task, such as many emails labeled spam or not spam.

2. Choose a type of model that suits the task.

3. Train the model: it makes predictions, compares them with the correct answers, and adjusts its internal numbers to make fewer mistakes. This repeats many times.

4. Test the model on new data it has never seen, to check that it really learned the pattern and did not just memorize the examples.

5. Deploy the model so it can handle real inputs.

6. Monitor results and retrain with better data when the model makes mistakes.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
AI can be grouped by ability:

1. Narrow AI: Built for one task or a small set of tasks, such as translating text or recommending videos. All AI in use today is narrow AI.

2. General AI: A hypothetical system that could learn and perform any intellectual task a human can. It does not exist yet.

AI can also be grouped by technique:

3. Supervised learning: Learns from examples that already have the correct answer.

4. Unsupervised learning: Finds hidden groups or patterns in data that has no answers.

5. Reinforcement learning: Learns by trial and error, receiving rewards for good actions.

6. Natural language processing: Lets computers work with human language.

7. Computer vision: Lets computers understand images and video.

8. Generative AI: Creates new text, images, audio or code from what it has learned.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
1. An email spam filter is trained on thousands of emails that people have already marked as spam or not spam. It learns which words and patterns suggest spam, then sorts new emails by itself.

2. A video app recommends what to watch next by learning from what similar users watched.

3. Face unlock on a phone compares the camera image with a stored face pattern.

4. Online translators convert text between languages.

5. A chatbot answers questions in natural language.

6. In hospitals, AI can help doctors spot signs of disease in X-ray images, but a doctor makes the final decision.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: AI is used in healthcare for medical images and drug research, in banks to detect fraud, in education for tutoring and feedback, and in farming to monitor crops. It is used in transport for navigation and driver-assistance features, in customer service for chatbots, and in cybersecurity to detect unusual activity on networks.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: AI can work quickly and without getting tired, and it can find patterns in amounts of data too large for people to check. It can automate repetitive tasks, give results around the clock, and in some narrow tasks it matches or exceeds human accuracy.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: AI is only as good as its data, so poor or unfair data leads to poor or unfair results. A model can be wrong while sounding confident, and generative AI can produce false information, so important results must be checked by people. Many models cannot explain why they gave an answer. AI raises privacy concerns, needs large amounts of energy and computing power to train, and changes the kind of work people do. Human oversight is necessary.

sections.content: Python Programming, Cloud Computing, Internet of Things, Cybersecurity, Data Structures and Algorithms.

title: Cloud Computing
description: An introduction to cloud computing, the delivery of servers, storage, databases and software over the internet, covering how it works, the IaaS, PaaS and SaaS service models, public, private and hybrid clouds, and its benefits and limits.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services, such as servers, storage, databases, networking and software, over the internet on demand. Instead of buying and running your own computers, you use the provider's computers and usually pay only for what you use. The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) describes five key traits: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.

sections.title: History
sections.content: The idea began in the 1960s with time-sharing, where many users shared one large computer, and John McCarthy suggested that computing might one day be sold like a public utility. In the 1990s, virtualization made it possible to split one physical machine into several virtual ones, and in 1999 Salesforce began delivering business software through a website. Amazon Web Services launched its storage service (S3) and its virtual servers (EC2) in 2006, which is widely seen as the start of modern cloud computing. Google App Engine followed in 2008, and Microsoft Azure became generally available in 2010.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Data center: A large building full of servers, storage and networking equipment, owned and run by the cloud provider.

2. Virtualization: Software that divides one physical server into several separate virtual machines.

3. On-demand self-service: You can create or remove resources yourself, in minutes, without talking to a person.

4. Elasticity and scalability: Resources can grow when demand is high and shrink when it is low.

5. Pay-as-you-go: Usage is measured, and you are charged for what you use.

6. Region: A geographic area where the provider keeps data centers. Choosing a region affects speed, cost and legal rules about where data is stored.

7. Shared responsibility: The provider protects the underlying infrastructure, while the customer is responsible for protecting their own data, accounts and settings.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. The provider builds data centers filled with servers, storage and network equipment.

2. Virtualization divides these machines into many virtual resources that can be given to different customers, a design called multi-tenancy.

3. A customer asks for a resource, such as a server or a database, through a website or a programming interface.

4. The system sets up the resource within minutes and connects it to the internet.

5. The customer uses it over the internet from any device.

6. The provider measures usage, such as hours of computing or amount of storage, and bills for it.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
Service models, from most control to least:

1. IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): You rent basic computing resources such as virtual servers and storage, and manage the software yourself. Example: Amazon EC2.

2. PaaS (Platform as a Service): You get a ready platform for building and running apps, and the provider manages the servers and system software. Example: Google App Engine.

3. SaaS (Software as a Service): You use finished software through a browser or app. Examples: Gmail and Microsoft 365.

Deployment models:

4. Public cloud: Shared services offered to many customers over the internet.

5. Private cloud: Cloud resources used by only one organization, in its own data center or a dedicated one.

6. Hybrid cloud: A mix of public and private clouds that work together.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
1. Email and file storage: Gmail and Google Drive keep your messages and files on the provider's servers, so you can open them from any device.

2. Video streaming: Netflix runs much of its service on Amazon Web Services, which lets it handle millions of viewers at once.

3. Development environments: GitHub Codespaces, the tool used to build this project, runs the code editor and the program on a cloud computer and shows it in a web browser. This is how a tablet can build and run a Java program.

4. A school website that gets very few visitors most of the year can add more servers for enrollment week and remove them afterward, paying only for the extra days.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Cloud computing is used for web hosting, storing and backing up files, building and testing software, streaming video and music, analyzing large amounts of data, and training AI models. Schools and companies use it for online classes, remote work and shared documents.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: There is no need to buy expensive equipment in advance, because you pay for what you use. Resources can be added within minutes and removed when no longer needed. Services can be reached from anywhere with internet. Providers handle maintenance, updates and backups, and large providers can offer high reliability by keeping copies of data in different locations.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: A reliable internet connection is required. Costs can grow quickly if usage is not watched. The customer has less control over the underlying hardware, and moving to another provider can be difficult, a problem called vendor lock-in. Security is shared, so a weak password or wrong setting by the customer can expose data. Laws may also limit where certain data can be stored. Provider outages, although rare, can affect many customers at the same time.

sections.content: Networking, Operating Systems, Cybersecurity, Artificial Intelligence, Internet of Things.

title: Internet of Things
description: An explanation of the Internet of Things (IoT): physical devices with sensors and network connections that send data and receive commands, covering the parts of an IoT system, communication methods such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, LoRaWAN and MQTT, a worked temperature-and-fan example, and the main security risks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of physical objects, called things, that contain sensors, a small processor and a network connection, so they can collect data, send it to other devices or to the cloud, and in many cases receive commands back. A thing can be as small as a temperature sensor on a farm or as large as a factory machine. What makes a device part of the IoT is that it exchanges data over a network without a person typing it in.

sections.title: History
sections.content: In 1982, students at Carnegie Mellon University connected a Coca-Cola vending machine to the internet so they could check from their computers whether a drink was available and cold, which is often cited as one of the first connected devices. In 1999, Kevin Ashton, working with the Auto-ID Center at MIT, used the phrase Internet of Things while describing how objects tagged with RFID chips could be tracked. In the same year, Andy Stanford-Clark and Arlen Nipper created MQTT, a lightweight messaging protocol that is still widely used. Around 2008 and 2009, estimates reported that more devices than people were connected to the internet. Cheap boards such as the Arduino and the ESP32 and low-cost sensors then made IoT projects possible for students and hobbyists.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Sensor: A component that measures something in the physical world and turns it into an electrical signal. Examples: a DHT22 for temperature and humidity, a PIR sensor for motion, and a GPS module for location.

2. Actuator: A component that does something in the physical world when it receives a command, such as a relay that switches a fan on, a motor, or a door lock.

3. Microcontroller: A small, low-power computer chip that reads sensors and controls actuators. Examples: Arduino boards and the ESP32, which also has built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. A Raspberry Pi is a larger single-board computer that can run a full operating system.

4. Connectivity: How the device reaches the network. Short range: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth Low Energy and Zigbee. Long range with very low power: LoRaWAN and NB-IoT. Wide area: cellular networks such as 4G and 5G.

5. Gateway: A device that collects data from many nearby sensors and forwards it to the internet.

6. Protocol: The agreed message format. MQTT uses a publish and subscribe model, in which devices publish messages to named topics on a server called a broker, and other devices subscribe to the topics they care about. HTTP and CoAP are also used.

7. Cloud platform: The online service that stores the data, analyzes it, and shows it in dashboards.

8. Edge computing: Processing data on or near the device, instead of sending everything to the cloud, to reduce delay and network traffic.

9. Firmware: The program stored inside the device. It must be updated over time to fix bugs and security flaws.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. A sensor measures a physical value, for example 28.5 degrees Celsius.

2. The microcontroller reads the value and may filter or average it.

3. The device connects to the network using Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, LoRaWAN or cellular.

4. It sends the reading using a protocol such as MQTT to a broker or a cloud platform.

5. The cloud stores the reading and compares it with rules or analyzes it, sometimes with machine learning.

6. If a rule matches, the system sends a command back to the device or sends an alert to a phone.

7. The actuator carries out the command, and the user can watch all of it on a dashboard or in an app.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
1. Consumer IoT: Smart speakers, smart lights and plugs, smart TVs, fitness bands and smartwatches.

2. Industrial IoT (IIoT): Sensors on factory machines that report vibration and temperature so repairs can be planned before a breakdown, and trackers on shipping containers.

3. Smart city IoT: Parking sensors, smart street lights, traffic monitoring and water meters.

4. Healthcare IoT: Wearable heart-rate monitors and connected glucose meters that send readings to a doctor.

5. Agricultural IoT: Soil-moisture sensors that tell a farm when to water, and weather stations.

6. Home and building automation: Thermostats, security cameras, door sensors and smoke alarms.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
A room temperature and fan system built with an ESP32:

1. A DHT22 sensor is connected to the ESP32. Every 10 seconds the ESP32 reads the temperature.

2. The ESP32 connects to the home Wi-Fi and publishes the reading to an MQTT broker:
```
Topic:   home/room1/temperature
Payload: 28.5
```

3. A rule on the server says: if the temperature is above 30, publish the command ON to the topic home/room1/fan.

4. A second ESP32 subscribed to home/room1/fan receives ON and switches a relay that powers a fan.

5. When the temperature falls below 28, the rule sends OFF, and the fan stops.

Other examples: a smart thermostat that learns when people are home, a wearable that sends heart-rate data to a phone, and soil-moisture sensors that start irrigation only when the soil is dry.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: IoT is used in smart homes, farming, manufacturing, logistics and fleet tracking, hospitals, energy meters, water monitoring and environmental monitoring. Cities use it for parking and traffic management, and businesses use it to monitor equipment and plan maintenance before machines fail.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: IoT gives real-time information about the physical world, so decisions are based on measurements instead of guesses. It automates routine tasks, such as watering or lighting, and can save energy and time. It supports early warnings, such as detecting a leak or a failing motor, and lets people monitor and control things remotely from a phone.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Security is the biggest concern. Many devices are sold with default passwords or no way to update their firmware, and attackers can control them. In 2016, the Mirai malware took over large numbers of cameras and routers with default passwords and used them to attack the DNS provider Dyn, which made many popular websites unreachable. Devices also collect personal information, which creates privacy risks. Different brands often do not work together because they use different standards. Small battery-powered devices must save energy, and a device that loses its network connection may stop working properly. Large systems also create large amounts of data that must be stored and analyzed.

sections.content: Cloud Computing, Networking, Wireless Networks, Cybersecurity, Artificial Intelligence.

title: Blockchain
description: An explanation of blockchain: a shared record made of blocks that are linked by cryptographic hashes and copied across many computers, covering how a transaction is verified and added, proof of work versus proof of stake, smart contracts, a worked hash-chain example, and its real limits.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A blockchain is a shared digital ledger, a list of records, in which the records are grouped into blocks and each block contains the cryptographic hash of the block before it. Because of this link, changing an old record changes its hash and breaks every block after it, which makes tampering easy to detect. The ledger is not kept in one place. Many computers, called nodes, each hold a copy and follow the same rules to agree on what is valid, so no single company or person has to be trusted to keep the record.

sections.title: History
sections.content: In 1991, Stuart Haber and W. Scott Stornetta described a way to timestamp documents by linking them with cryptography so they could not be changed without detection. On 31 October 2008, a person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto published the paper Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, and the Bitcoin network started on 3 January 2009 with its first block, called the genesis block. Ethereum, proposed by Vitalik Buterin, launched in 2015 and added smart contracts, which are programs that run on the blockchain. In 2016, a flaw in a smart contract called The DAO was exploited and about 3.6 million ether was taken, which showed that code errors cannot be easily undone. In September 2022, Ethereum changed its method of agreeing on blocks from proof of work to proof of stake, which reduced its energy use. Companies also built private blockchains, such as Hyperledger Fabric.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Block: A group of records, such as transactions, together with a timestamp and the hash of the previous block.

2. Hash: A fixed-length fingerprint created from data by a hash function. Bitcoin uses SHA-256, which produces 64 hexadecimal characters. The same input always gives the same hash, and changing even one character of the input gives a completely different hash.

3. Chain: Each block stores the previous block's hash, so the blocks form a sequence that cannot be reordered or edited without changing every later hash.

4. Node: A computer that keeps a copy of the blockchain and checks new blocks against the rules.

5. Digital signature: A user signs a transaction with a private key, and anyone can check the signature with the matching public key. This proves who authorized the transaction without revealing the private key.

6. Wallet: Software or a device that stores private keys. Whoever has the private key controls the funds, and a lost key cannot be recovered.

7. Consensus: The method nodes use to agree on the next block. The two best-known are proof of work and proof of stake.

8. Smart contract: A program stored on the blockchain that runs automatically when its conditions are met.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. A user creates a transaction, for example sending a coin to another user, and signs it with their private key.

2. The transaction is broadcast to the nodes of the network.

3. Nodes check that the signature is valid and that the sender really has the funds.

4. Valid transactions are collected into a candidate block.

5. Consensus decides who adds the next block. In proof of work, miners repeatedly change a number called a nonce until the block's hash meets a difficulty target, which takes a lot of computing power. Bitcoin aims for a new block about every 10 minutes. In proof of stake, a validator is selected based on the amount of cryptocurrency it has locked up as a deposit, and it can lose that deposit for cheating.

6. The new block, containing the hash of the previous block, is sent to all nodes, which check it and add it to their copy.

7. The transaction is confirmed. Each additional block placed on top makes it harder to change.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
1. Public blockchains: Anyone can read them and take part. Examples: Bitcoin and Ethereum.

2. Private blockchains: Run by one organization, which decides who can take part.

3. Consortium blockchains: Run by a group of organizations, such as several banks. Example: Hyperledger Fabric.

4. Hybrid blockchains: Combine private and public parts.

By consensus method: proof of work (Bitcoin) and proof of stake (Ethereum since 2022).

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
A simplified chain of three blocks. The hash values below are made up for illustration:
```
Block 1  data: Ana pays Ben 5   hash: A1F3   previous: 0000
Block 2  data: Ben pays Cy 2    hash: 7B9C   previous: A1F3
Block 3  data: Cy pays Dee 1    hash: 3E52   previous: 7B9C
```

If someone edits Block 1 to say Ana pays Ben 500, the hash of Block 1 changes. Block 2 still stores the old hash A1F3, so the link no longer matches and the change is detected. To hide it, the attacker would have to recompute every later block and also convince most of the network to accept the new version, which is extremely hard on a large network.

A real hash example: the SHA-256 hash of the text hello is 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824. If you change one letter, the new hash looks completely different.

A smart contract example: a contract can hold a payment and release it to a seller automatically once a delivery is confirmed.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Blockchain is used for cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, for tracking products through a supply chain, for checking the authenticity of certificates and records, for sending payments across borders, and for smart contracts in decentralized finance. Some organizations also use it to prove the origin of food or goods and to keep shared records between companies that do not fully trust each other.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: Records are tamper-evident, because changes break the chain. The data is shared, so there is no single point of failure and no single owner who can quietly change it. Transactions can be traced and audited, and people can transact directly without relying on a central intermediary.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Proof of work uses large amounts of electricity. Blockchains are slower than centralized databases, because every node must check every block, and Bitcoin handles only a few transactions per second. Data written to the chain is hard to remove, so mistakes and illegal content cannot be easily undone. A lost private key means lost funds, and a stolen key lets a thief spend them. Bugs in smart contracts can be exploited, as in The DAO. If one group controls more than half of a network's power, it can rewrite recent blocks, an attack called a 51 percent attack. Many problems that are said to need a blockchain can be solved more simply with an ordinary database, so it is not always the right tool.

sections.title: Related Topics
sections.content: Cryptography, Cybersecurity, Networking, Database Management, Cloud Computing.

title: JavaScript
description: An introduction to JavaScript, the programming language that makes web pages interactive, covering variables, data types, functions, the DOM, events, asynchronous code with promises and fetch, where JavaScript runs, and how it differs from Java.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: JavaScript is a programming language that runs in every major web browser and is used to make web pages interactive: reacting to clicks, changing what is shown without reloading the page, checking forms, and loading data from servers. It is also used outside the browser, for servers and apps. JavaScript is dynamically typed, which means a variable can hold different kinds of values at different times, and the type is checked while the program runs. Despite the similar name, JavaScript and Java are different languages.

sections.title: History
sections.content: Brendan Eich created JavaScript at Netscape in May 1995, reportedly in about ten days. It was first called Mocha, then LiveScript, and was renamed JavaScript in December 1995 as part of a marketing agreement with Sun Microsystems, the company that created Java. In 1997, the language was standardized by Ecma International as ECMAScript (ECMA-262). The 2015 edition, known as ES6 or ES2015, added let and const, arrow functions, classes, modules and promises, and new editions have been published every year since. In 2009, Ryan Dahl released Node.js, which lets JavaScript run on servers outside the browser.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Variables: Named storage for values. Use let for a value that can change and const for a value that must not be reassigned. The older keyword var is still found in old code.

2. Data types: JavaScript has eight: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol, and object. Arrays and functions are kinds of objects.

3. Functions: Reusable blocks of code. Functions are values, so they can be stored in variables, passed to other functions and returned from them.

4. Objects and arrays: An object stores named properties, such as a student with a name and a course. An array stores an ordered list.

5. DOM (Document Object Model): The browser's tree of objects that represents the HTML page. JavaScript changes the page by changing the DOM.

6. Events: Things that happen on the page, such as a click, a key press or a form submission. You attach a function, called an event listener, that runs when the event happens.

7. Asynchronous programming: Tasks that take time, such as loading data from a server, run in the background so the page does not freeze. They are handled with callbacks, promises, or the async and await keywords.

8. Event loop: The mechanism that lets JavaScript, which runs one task at a time on a single thread, still handle events and background tasks without blocking.

9. Equality: Use === (strict equality), which compares value and type. The == operator converts types first and can give surprising results.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. The browser downloads the HTML page and finds the script, either written inside the page or in a separate .js file.

2. The browser's JavaScript engine reads and runs the code. Chrome and Edge use V8, Firefox uses SpiderMonkey, and Safari uses JavaScriptCore. Modern engines compile the code to machine code while it runs, which is called just-in-time compilation.

3. The code reads and changes the DOM, so the visible page updates immediately.

4. When the user clicks or types, the browser creates an event, and the matching listener function runs.

5. When the code needs data from a server, it sends a request with fetch. The page keeps working, and a function runs when the response arrives.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
Where JavaScript runs:

1. In the browser (client side): Controls page behavior. This is its original use.

2. On the server: Node.js, Deno and Bun run JavaScript outside a browser to build web servers and tools.

3. In apps: Electron builds desktop apps, and React Native builds mobile apps, using JavaScript.

Related tools:

4. Libraries and frameworks: React, Vue and Angular help build large interfaces.

5. TypeScript: A language built on JavaScript that adds types and is converted to JavaScript before it runs.

sections.title: Examples
Applications
sections.content: JavaScript is used in nearly every website for menus, forms, animations and live updates. It powers web apps such as online documents, chat and maps, and it is used on servers with Node.js. It is also used to build desktop and mobile apps, browser extensions and games, and the Search IT website in this project uses it to search and show articles.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: It runs in every browser with nothing to install, so it is easy to start with. It is the only language browsers run directly, and a very large number of libraries and learning resources exist. The same language can be used on the page and on the server. It can update a page without reloading it.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Because types are checked only when the program runs, mistakes such as using the wrong kind of value can appear late. Automatic type conversion can give confusing results, which is why === is recommended. Long calculations can freeze a page because JavaScript runs on one thread. Code that puts user input directly into a page can allow cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks. The many frameworks change quickly, so there is a lot to keep up with.

sections.content: HTML and CSS, REST APIs and JSON, Web Development, Java Programming, Python Programming.

title: Data Structures and Algorithms
description: An explanation of data structures (ways to organize data such as arrays, stacks, queues, hash tables and trees) and algorithms (step-by-step methods such as searching and sorting), with Big O notation and worked Java examples of binary search, a stack and bubble sort.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A data structure is a way of organizing and storing data in a computer so that it can be used efficiently. An algorithm is a finite, step-by-step set of instructions that solves a problem or completes a task. The two work together: the structure you choose decides how fast and how simply an algorithm can find, add or remove data. Studying them teaches you to compare different solutions to the same problem by how much time and memory they need.

sections.title: History
sections.content: The word algorithm comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, a mathematician who wrote in Baghdad in the 9th century. One of the oldest known algorithms, Euclid's method for finding the greatest common divisor of two numbers, dates to about 300 BC. Computer science added new ones: Tony Hoare invented quicksort in 1959, and Edsger Dijkstra devised his shortest-path algorithm in 1956. Donald Knuth began publishing The Art of Computer Programming in 1968, which set out how to analyze algorithms carefully. Today every major programming language ships ready-made data structures, such as the Java Collections Framework.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Data structure: A way to organize data, such as an array, list, stack, queue, hash table or tree.

2. Algorithm: A clear, finite sequence of steps that always produces a result for valid input.

3. Time complexity: How the number of steps grows as the amount of data (n) grows.

4. Space complexity: How much extra memory an algorithm needs as n grows.

5. Big O notation: A way to describe the growth of time or space in the worst case, ignoring small details. Common classes, from fastest to slowest growth: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n), and O(n squared) quadratic.

6. Abstract data type: A description of what a structure does, such as a stack with push and pop, separate from how it is built inside.

7. Trade-off: No structure is best for everything. One may be fast to read but slow to insert, so you choose the one that matches how your program uses the data.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. Define the problem clearly, including the input and the expected output.

2. Choose a data structure that fits how the data will be used. For example, use a hash table when you must look items up by key.

3. Design an algorithm, either from a known method or by breaking the problem into smaller steps.

4. Trace the algorithm by hand on a small example to check that it is correct.

5. Estimate its Big O time and memory use.

6. Write the code, test it with normal, empty and unusual inputs, and compare it with other solutions if it is too slow.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
Common data structures:

1. Array: A fixed-size, ordered block of items. Reading an item by its index is O(1).

2. ArrayList: A resizable array in Java. Reading by index is O(1), and adding at the end is usually O(1).

3. Linked list: Items connected by links. Inserting after a known item is O(1), but finding an item is O(n).

4. Stack: Last in, first out (LIFO). Operations: push and pop. Used for undo and the back button.

5. Queue: First in, first out (FIFO). Used for print jobs and waiting lines.

6. Hash table (Java HashMap): Stores key-value pairs. Lookup, insert and delete are O(1) on average.

7. Tree: Items arranged in parent and child levels. A balanced binary search tree finds an item in O(log n).

8. Graph: Items (nodes) connected by links (edges), such as a map of roads.

Common algorithms:

9. Searching: Linear search checks each item, O(n). Binary search halves a sorted list each step, O(log n).

10. Sorting: Bubble sort is simple but O(n squared). Merge sort is O(n log n). Quicksort is O(n log n) on average.

11. Graph algorithms: Breadth-first search, depth-first search and Dijkstra's shortest path.

12. Techniques: Recursion, divide and conquer, greedy algorithms and dynamic programming.

sections.title: Examples
Applications
sections.content: Search engines and databases use trees and hash tables to find records quickly, and database indexes are usually built on trees. Maps and navigation apps use graph algorithms to find routes. Operating systems use queues to schedule programs, text editors use stacks for undo, and compilers use trees to understand code. Games, social networks, online shops and AI programs all depend on well-chosen data structures and algorithms.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: Choosing the right structure and algorithm can make a program thousands of times faster and make it use less memory. Knowing them helps you compare solutions with Big O instead of guessing, write cleaner code, and prepare for technical interviews, where these topics are common. The ideas apply in every programming language.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: There is no single best structure, so choosing needs thought about how the data will be used. Big O describes how running time grows and ignores constant factors, so a simpler O(n squared) method can be faster than a complex O(n log n) method on small data. Worst-case and average-case speed can differ, as with quicksort. Complex structures are harder to write and debug, and for small programs a plain array or ArrayList is often enough.

sections.content: Introduction to Programming, Java Programming, Python Programming, Database Management, Artificial Intelligence.
