title: Git and GitHub
description: An explanation of Git, the version control system that records every change to a project, and GitHub, the website that hosts Git repositories, covering commits, the staging area, branches, merging, remotes, the everyday commands add, commit and push, and how to keep secrets out of a repository.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Git is a free, distributed version control system. It records the history of a project as a series of saved snapshots called commits, so you can see what changed, who changed it and when, and return to an earlier version if something breaks. GitHub is a separate website and service that stores Git repositories online, so that people can back up their work, share it and work on it together. Git is the tool, and GitHub is one of the places that hosts it.

sections.title: History
sections.content: Linus Torvalds created Git in April 2005 to manage the development of the Linux kernel, after the commercial tool that the Linux developers had been using became unavailable to them. He designed it to be fast, to work without a central server, and to keep the history safe. GitHub was launched in April 2008 by Tom Preston-Werner, Chris Wanstrath and PJ Hyett, and it became the most widely used place to host code. Microsoft announced in 2018 that it would buy GitHub for 7.5 billion US dollars. In 2020, GitHub changed the default name of the first branch of new repositories from master to main.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Repository (repo): A project folder together with its complete history, stored in a hidden folder named .git.

2. Commit: A saved snapshot of the project with a message that explains the change. Each commit has a unique ID, a 40-character hash.

3. Working directory: The files you see and edit.

4. Staging area: A holding area where you choose which changes will go into the next commit. The command git add puts changes there.

5. Branch: A separate line of development. You can try a new feature on a branch without disturbing the main code.

6. Merge: Combining the changes of one branch into another. If both branches changed the same lines, a merge conflict occurs and you must choose the correct result by hand.

7. Remote: A copy of the repository stored elsewhere, such as on GitHub. The default remote is named origin.

8. Clone, push and pull: Clone downloads a full copy of a repository. Push uploads your commits to a remote. Pull downloads new commits from a remote and combines them with yours.

9. Pull request: A request on GitHub to merge one branch into another, where teammates can review and discuss the changes first.

10. .gitignore: A file that lists files and folders Git must not track, such as passwords, build output and personal settings.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. You edit files in the working directory.

2. You run git status to see which files changed.

3. You run git add to move the chosen changes into the staging area.

4. You run git commit with a message. Git saves a snapshot of everything that was staged and gives it a hash.

5. Each commit points to the commit before it, which forms the history of the project.

6. You run git push to upload the new commits to the remote repository on GitHub.

7. Other people run git pull to receive them. Because every copy holds the full history, work can continue offline and any copy can restore the project.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
1. Local version control: Keeps versions only on one computer.

2. Centralized version control: A single central server holds the history, as in Subversion. Everyone must connect to it.

3. Distributed version control: Every user has a full copy of the history. Git and Mercurial work this way.

Services that host Git repositories: GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket.

Common ways of working: committing directly to the main branch for solo projects, creating a branch for each feature, or forking a repository to your own account and proposing changes through a pull request.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
1. The everyday cycle used to save work to GitHub:
```
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Add SQL Basics article"
git push
```
The first command lists what changed, the second stages everything, the third saves a snapshot with a clear message, and the last uploads it.

2. Working on a feature in a branch, then merging it:
```
git switch -c add-articles
git add .
git commit -m "Add new articles"
git switch main
git merge add-articles
```

3. Looking at the history and the last change:
```
git log --oneline
git diff
```

4. Keeping a private folder out of the repository. Add this line to .gitignore:
```
data/
```
If a file was already tracked, git rm --cached stops Git from tracking it. This is how the Search IT project keeps its accounts file, which contains password hashes, out of GitHub. Note that a file that was uploaded before stays in the old history, so a real password that was ever committed must be changed.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Git is used by almost all software teams to track changes and work together without overwriting each other. Students use it to submit and back up projects, open-source projects use GitHub to accept contributions from anyone, and writers and designers use it for text and configuration files. GitHub also provides issue tracking, project boards, automatic testing and free hosting for websites with GitHub Pages.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: Nothing is lost: any earlier version can be restored. You can see who changed each line and why. Branches let people experiment safely, and many people can work on the same project at once. Because every copy has the full history, work is backed up in several places and most commands work without internet.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Git has a learning curve, because of ideas such as staging and branches and because commands can be confusing at first. Merge conflicts must be solved by hand. Git works best with text files and is less suited to very large files or many binary files. Mistakes, such as committing a password or a large file, are hard to fully remove from history. Anything pushed to a public repository can be seen by everyone, so private data must never be committed.

title: Computer Hardware
description: An explanation of computer hardware: the physical parts of a computer, including the CPU, RAM, storage (HDD and SSD), motherboard, GPU, power supply and input and output devices, how they work together to run a program, and how to read a computer's specifications.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Computer hardware is the physical parts of a computer system, the components you can touch, such as the processor, memory, storage, motherboard, screen and keyboard. Hardware does nothing useful alone. It needs software, which is the programs and data that tell the hardware what to do. Every computer, from a phone to a large server, is built from the same kinds of hardware components.

sections.title: History
sections.content: In 1837, Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, a mechanical machine with a processing unit and a memory, though it was never finished. The ENIAC, completed in 1945 in the United States, used about 17,000 vacuum tubes and filled a large room. The transistor was invented at Bell Labs in 1947, and it replaced vacuum tubes with smaller, cooler and more reliable parts. Jack Kilby demonstrated the first integrated circuit in 1958, which put several transistors on one chip. In 1971, Intel released the 4004, the first commercial microprocessor, which placed a whole processor on one chip. The IBM Personal Computer arrived in 1981. In 1965, Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling roughly every two years, an observation called Moore's law, and it held for decades. Solid-state drives (SSDs) based on flash memory gradually replaced hard disks in laptops and many desktops in the 2010s.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. CPU (central processing unit): The processor, the part that runs program instructions. It is described by its number of cores (each core can work on a task), its clock speed in gigahertz (GHz, billions of cycles per second), and its cache, a very small, very fast memory inside the chip.

2. RAM (random access memory): The computer's short-term working memory. It holds the programs and data that are in use right now and is much faster than storage. It is volatile, which means its contents are lost when the power is turned off. Sizes are measured in gigabytes (GB), and common types are DDR4 and DDR5.

3. Storage: Keeps programs and files permanently, even without power (non-volatile). A hard disk drive (HDD) stores data on spinning magnetic platters. A solid-state drive (SSD) stores data in flash chips with no moving parts.

4. Motherboard: The main circuit board that connects the CPU, RAM, storage and other parts, and carries the signals between them.

5. GPU (graphics processing unit): A processor specialized for drawing images and doing many simple calculations at once. It is used for games, video editing and training AI models.

6. Power supply unit (PSU): Converts the electricity from the wall socket into the lower voltages the components need.

7. Firmware: Small permanent software stored on a chip on the motherboard, called BIOS or UEFI, that starts the computer and loads the operating system.

8. Fetch, decode, execute: The cycle the CPU repeats billions of times per second. It fetches an instruction from memory, decodes what it means, and executes it.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. When you press the power button, the power supply delivers electricity to the motherboard and all components.

2. The firmware (UEFI or BIOS) runs a self-test, called POST, to check that the CPU, RAM and other basic parts respond.

3. The firmware finds the operating system on the storage drive and copies the first part of it into RAM.

4. The CPU fetches instructions from RAM, decodes them, executes them, and writes results back to RAM. Frequently used data is kept in the fast cache.

5. When you open a program or a file, it is copied from the storage drive into RAM so the CPU can reach it quickly.

6. Input devices, such as a keyboard or touchscreen, send signals to the CPU. Output devices, such as the screen or speakers, receive the results. The GPU prepares the picture that appears on the screen.

7. When you save a file, the data is written from RAM to the storage drive so it is kept after the power is turned off.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
1. Input devices: Send data into the computer. Examples: keyboard, mouse, touchscreen, microphone, scanner and webcam.

2. Output devices: Present results. Examples: monitor, printer and speakers.

3. Processing devices: The CPU and the GPU.

4. Memory: RAM for working memory, cache inside the CPU, and ROM, which holds fixed firmware.

5. Storage devices: Hard disk drives, solid-state drives, USB flash drives, memory cards and optical discs.

6. Communication devices: A network interface card (NIC), a Wi-Fi adapter, Bluetooth and a modem, which connect the computer to networks.

Kinds of computers: desktop computers, laptops, tablets, smartphones, servers and embedded computers inside appliances and cars.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
1. Reading a specification. A laptop is listed as: Intel Core i5, 8 cores, 3.0 GHz, 16 GB DDR4 RAM, 512 GB SSD. This means a processor with 8 cores that runs at 3.0 billion cycles per second, 16 GB of working memory so several programs can be open at once, and 512 GB of permanent storage on a fast flash drive.

2. Comparing storage types:
```
Type        How it stores        Typical speed        Moving parts
HDD         Magnetic platters    about 100-150 MB/s   Yes
SATA SSD    Flash chips          about 500 MB/s       No
NVMe SSD    Flash chips          several GB/s         No
```
An SSD makes a computer start and open programs much faster than an HDD.

3. Why more RAM helps: if the programs you use need more memory than you have, the operating system moves data to the much slower storage drive, and the computer becomes slow. Adding RAM prevents this.

4. A tablet combines a processor, memory, flash storage, a touchscreen, a camera, a battery and wireless chips on one small board. A desktop computer uses the same kinds of parts, but as separate, replaceable components.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Knowing hardware helps you choose a computer for a task. Office work and web browsing need a modest CPU, 8 GB of RAM and an SSD. Programming with a code editor and several tools open is more comfortable with 16 GB of RAM. Video editing, 3D design and gaming need a strong CPU and a dedicated GPU. Servers need many cores, large RAM and reliable storage. It also helps you troubleshoot problems, such as a computer that is slow because of a nearly full drive or too little RAM.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: Modern hardware is far faster, smaller and cheaper than earlier generations. Parts follow common standards, so many components can be upgraded or replaced separately, for example adding RAM or swapping a hard disk for an SSD. Solid-state storage is quiet, fast and more resistant to shocks.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Hardware wears out and becomes outdated, and heat is a constant problem, because fast processors need cooling. Batteries lose capacity over time. Some devices, especially thin laptops and tablets, have parts that cannot be upgraded. Power use and cost grow with performance, and discarded electronics create electronic waste that must be recycled properly. Parts must also be compatible with each other, such as the right type of RAM for the motherboard.

title: DNS (Domain Name System)
description: An explanation of the Domain Name System (DNS), the internet service that translates domain names such as www.example.com into IP addresses, covering the DNS hierarchy, resolvers and name servers, common record types, caching and TTL, a step-by-step lookup, and DNS security problems.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The Domain Name System (DNS) is the internet's naming service. It translates human-friendly domain names, such as www.example.com, into the numeric IP addresses that computers use to find each other, such as 203.0.113.10. It is often compared to a phone book, because you look up a name and get a number. DNS is a hierarchical and distributed system, which means no single computer holds all the answers. The information is spread across millions of servers around the world.

sections.title: History
sections.content: In the early days of the ARPANET, every computer name and address was listed in a single file called HOSTS.TXT, maintained by the Stanford Research Institute and copied by everyone. As the network grew, this became impossible to keep up to date. In 1983, Paul Mockapetris designed DNS, first described in RFC 882 and RFC 883, and the design was refined in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 in 1987, which are still the base of the system. ICANN was created in 1998 to coordinate domain names and IP addresses. DNSSEC, a set of security extensions, was standardized in 2005, and DNS over HTTPS, which encrypts DNS queries, was standardized in 2018 in RFC 8484.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Domain name: A name that identifies a site or service, read from right to left in levels. In www.example.com, com is the top-level domain, example is the second-level domain, and www is a subdomain.

2. DNS hierarchy: At the top is the root, then top-level domains (TLDs) such as .com and .org and country codes such as .ph, then individual domains and subdomains.

3. Root name servers: The servers at the top of the hierarchy. They know where to find the servers for each TLD. There are 13 named root server addresses, labeled A to M, run by 12 organizations, and each is copied at hundreds of sites around the world.

4. Authoritative name server: The server that holds the official records for a domain and gives the final answer for it.

5. Recursive resolver: The server that does the searching for you. It is usually provided by your internet provider, or you can use a public one such as 8.8.8.8 (Google) or 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare).

6. DNS records: The entries stored for a domain. A maps a name to an IPv4 address. AAAA maps to an IPv6 address. CNAME makes one name an alias of another. MX names the mail servers. NS names the domain's name servers. TXT holds text, often used for verification. PTR maps an address back to a name.

7. TTL (time to live): The number of seconds that an answer may be kept in a cache before it must be looked up again.

8. Caching: Storing recent answers on your device, in your browser and in the resolver, so repeated lookups are instant.

9. Port 53: DNS normally uses port 53, over UDP for short queries and TCP for large answers.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
When you type www.example.com into a browser:

1. The browser and the operating system check their caches. If the address is stored and still valid, the lookup ends here.

2. If not, the computer sends a query to the recursive resolver.

3. If the resolver has no cached answer, it asks a root server, which replies with the address of the servers for the .com TLD.

4. The resolver asks a .com TLD server, which replies with the address of the authoritative name server for example.com.

5. The resolver asks that authoritative server for www.example.com and receives the IP address.

6. The resolver caches the answer for the length of its TTL and returns it to your computer.

7. The browser connects to the IP address and requests the web page.

The whole lookup usually takes only a few milliseconds to a few tens of milliseconds.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
Types of DNS servers:

1. Recursive resolvers: Look up answers on behalf of users.

2. Root servers: Point to the TLD servers.

3. TLD servers: Know the name servers of every domain under a TLD such as .com.

4. Authoritative servers: Hold the real records for a domain.

Types of queries: A recursive query asks a server to find the full answer itself. An iterative query lets a server answer with the best information it has, such as a referral to the next server.

Security and privacy variants: DNSSEC adds digital signatures that prove an answer is genuine. DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) encrypt queries so that others on the network cannot read them.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
1. Looking up a name with the nslookup tool. The address shown is a reserved example address, used for illustration:
```
nslookup example.com
Name:    example.com
Address: 203.0.113.10
```

2. Records in a domain's zone. Each line gives the name, the TTL in seconds, the record type and the value:
```
example.com.      3600  IN  A      203.0.113.10
www.example.com.  3600  IN  CNAME  example.com.
example.com.      3600  IN  MX 10  mail.example.com.
```
The A record gives the address, the CNAME makes www an alias of the main name, and the MX record says where email for the domain is delivered.

3. The name localhost is not looked up on the internet. Your computer's hosts file maps it to 127.0.0.1, the address of the computer itself. This is why the Search IT server at http://localhost:8080 works without any DNS server.

4. Moving a website to a new server: the owner changes the A record to the new address. Because of caching, some users see the new server immediately and others only after the old TTL expires.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: DNS is used every time a browser, app or game reaches a named server, which makes it essential to the web, email and nearly all online services. Companies use DNS to send visitors to the nearest server, spread traffic across several servers, and move services without changing the name. DNS filtering is used by schools, families and companies to block harmful or unwanted sites. Email systems depend on MX and TXT records to deliver mail and fight spam.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: People can use easy-to-remember names instead of numbers. A site can change its server or IP address without telling its visitors, because only the DNS record changes. The distributed design and caching make lookups fast and let the system serve billions of users without one central point that could fail.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: If DNS fails, websites become unreachable even though their servers are working. Traditional DNS queries are not encrypted, so others on the network can see which sites you look up. Attackers can attempt DNS spoofing or cache poisoning, which gives users a false address that leads to a fake site, and security researcher Dan Kaminsky demonstrated a serious cache poisoning flaw in 2008. DNS servers can be flooded with traffic, as in the 2016 attack on the provider Dyn, which made many popular sites unreachable. Because of caching, changes to a record can take hours to reach everyone.

title: Wireless Networks
description: An explanation of wireless networks, which connect devices with radio waves instead of cables, covering Wi-Fi standards and frequency bands, access points, how a device joins and sends data, Bluetooth, cellular and other wireless types, security (WPA2 and WPA3), and the common limits of range and interference.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A wireless network connects devices using radio waves instead of cables. The most common example is Wi-Fi, which lets laptops, phones and tablets join a local network and the internet without plugging in a cable. Other wireless technologies include Bluetooth, which connects nearby accessories, and cellular networks (4G and 5G), which cover large areas. Wireless networks still depend on wired connections behind the scenes, since the access point or tower is usually connected to the rest of the network by a cable.

sections.title: History
sections.content: In 1971, Norman Abramson and his team at the University of Hawaii created ALOHAnet, the first wireless packet network, to link computers on different islands by radio. In 1997, the IEEE published the first 802.11 standard for wireless local area networks, with a speed of up to 2 Mbps. In 1999, the faster 802.11b (11 Mbps) and 802.11a (54 Mbps) were released, and the industry group now called the Wi-Fi Alliance introduced the name Wi-Fi. Later versions include 802.11n in 2009, 802.11ac in 2013 and 802.11ax in 2019, and from 2018 the generations have been numbered Wi-Fi 4, 5 and 6, with Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) following. Cellular networks moved from 2G digital voice in the early 1990s, to 3G data around 2001, to 4G LTE around 2010, and to 5G from 2019.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Radio frequency bands: Wi-Fi uses 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz and, in newer versions, 6 GHz. Lower frequencies travel farther and pass through walls better, and higher frequencies carry more data over shorter distances.

2. Access point (AP): The device that connects wireless devices to the network. A home wireless router combines an access point, a router and a small switch in one box.

3. SSID: The name of a wireless network, which is what you see in the list of networks.

4. Channel: A slice of a frequency band. Neighboring networks on the same or overlapping channels interfere with each other. In the 2.4 GHz band, only channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap.

5. Signal strength: Measured in dBm, a negative number. Closer to zero is stronger, so minus 50 dBm is a very strong signal and minus 80 dBm is weak.

6. Bandwidth and throughput: Bandwidth is the maximum speed the link supports, and throughput is the real speed you get, which is lower because of distance, interference, overhead and the number of users sharing the connection.

7. Encryption and authentication: A password and an encryption standard, WPA2 or WPA3, make sure only authorized devices join and that the data cannot be read by others.

8. CSMA/CA: The rule wireless devices follow to avoid collisions. Each device listens first and transmits only when the channel is free.

9. Infrastructure and ad hoc modes: In infrastructure mode, devices connect through an access point. In ad hoc mode, devices connect directly to each other.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. The access point broadcasts its SSID, and the device scans and lists the networks it hears.

2. The user selects a network and enters the password. The device and the access point perform a handshake that proves the password is correct and creates encryption keys.

3. The device is now associated with the access point. A DHCP server, usually in the router, gives it an IP address.

4. When the device sends data, it breaks it into frames, checks that the channel is free, encrypts the frames, and transmits them as radio waves.

5. The access point receives the frames, decrypts them and forwards the data to the router and the internet.

6. Replies travel the same way in reverse. If the signal gets weak, the device may switch to a stronger access point, which is called roaming.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
By area covered:

1. Wireless personal area network (WPAN): A few meters. Bluetooth, Zigbee and NFC.

2. Wireless local area network (WLAN): A home, school or office, typically tens of meters indoors. Wi-Fi.

3. Wireless wide area network (WWAN): Kilometers. Cellular networks such as 4G LTE and 5G.

4. Low-power wide-area networks (LPWAN): Long range with very little power, for sensors. LoRaWAN and NB-IoT.

5. Satellite networks: Used where no other coverage exists, such as ships, remote areas and aircraft.

Wi-Fi generations, with the highest theoretical speeds (real speeds are lower):
```
Name     Standard     Year   Bands                Top speed (theory)
Wi-Fi 4  802.11n      2009   2.4 and 5 GHz        600 Mbps
Wi-Fi 5  802.11ac     2013   5 GHz                several Gbps
Wi-Fi 6  802.11ax     2019   2.4 and 5 GHz        9.6 Gbps
Wi-Fi 6E 802.11ax     2020   adds 6 GHz           9.6 Gbps
Wi-Fi 7  802.11be     2024   2.4, 5 and 6 GHz     46 Gbps
```

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
1. Joining a home network: your tablet lists the SSIDs it hears, you choose one, you type the password, and within seconds the router gives the tablet an IP address and it can open websites.

2. Choosing a band. A router offers a 2.4 GHz and a 5 GHz network.
```
2.4 GHz: longer range, passes through walls better, slower, crowded
5 GHz:   shorter range, faster, less crowded
```
Use 5 GHz when you are in the same room as the router and 2.4 GHz when you are far away or behind walls.

3. Bluetooth connects wireless earphones to a phone over a few meters, using very little power.

4. A phone sends mobile data through a cellular tower, which can be several kilometers away.

5. Basic safe setup for a home router: choose WPA3 if all devices support it, otherwise WPA2 with AES, use a long password, change the default administrator password of the router, and turn off WPS.

6. Cloud tools such as the one used to build this project depend on a stable connection. A weak Wi-Fi signal can drop the connection to the online code editor.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Wireless networks are used in homes, schools and offices for laptops, phones and tablets, and in public places such as airports, cafes and libraries. Bluetooth connects headphones, keyboards, speakers and smartwatches. Cellular networks provide mobile calls and mobile internet. Wireless links are also used in smart homes, warehouses, hospitals and factories, in the Internet of Things, in vehicles, and in places where laying cables is difficult or costly.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: Users can move around while staying connected. Installation is faster and cheaper than running cables, and new devices can be added easily without new wiring. Wireless access reaches places where cables are impractical, and it supports modern devices such as phones, tablets and sensors that have no cable port.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Range is limited, and walls, floors, metal and water reduce the signal. Interference from other networks, microwave ovens and Bluetooth devices can slow the connection. Speed and delay are usually worse than a wired Ethernet connection, and all devices on one access point share the same airtime. Because radio waves can be received by anyone nearby, security is a concern. Open networks send data that others can capture, the old WEP encryption is broken, and in 2017 a flaw called KRACK was found in WPA2, which was fixed by updates. Always use the latest security standard and keep router firmware updated.

title: Network Security
description: An explanation of network security: the tools and practices that protect a network and its data from unauthorized access and attacks, covering the CIA triad, firewalls, intrusion detection and prevention, VPNs, authentication, segmentation, common attacks such as DDoS and man-in-the-middle, and a sample firewall rule set.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Network security is the set of policies, tools and practices used to protect a computer network and the data that travels across it from unauthorized access, misuse, damage and attack. Its goals are summarized by the CIA triad: confidentiality (only authorized people can read the data), integrity (the data cannot be changed without detection) and availability (the network and its services work when they are needed). Good network security uses several layers of protection together instead of relying on a single tool.

sections.title: History
sections.content: On 2 November 1988, the Morris worm spread across the early internet and slowed or crashed about 10 percent of the roughly 60,000 connected computers. This was a turning point that led to the creation of the first computer emergency response team and to wider use of network defenses. Packet-filtering firewalls were developed in the late 1980s and became common in the 1990s. Netscape introduced SSL in 1995, which was later standardized as TLS in 1999 and is what makes HTTPS secure. Wi-Fi security moved from WEP (1997), which was broken, to WPA (2003), WPA2 (2004) and WPA3 (2018). In 2010, John Kindervag of Forrester Research described the zero trust model, which says that no user or device should be trusted automatically just because it is inside the network.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. CIA triad: Confidentiality, integrity and availability, the three goals of security.

2. Threat, vulnerability and risk: A threat is something that can cause harm, such as an attacker. A vulnerability is a weakness, such as unpatched software or a weak password. Risk is the chance that a threat uses a vulnerability, multiplied by the damage it would cause.

3. Firewall: A system that allows or blocks network traffic according to rules about source, destination, port and protocol.

4. IDS and IPS: An intrusion detection system (IDS) watches traffic and raises alerts about suspicious activity. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) can also block it automatically.

5. VPN (virtual private network): Creates an encrypted tunnel across a public network so that data cannot be read on the way.

6. Authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA): Proving who you are, deciding what you may do, and recording what you did. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires two or more proofs, such as a password and a code from a phone.

7. Network segmentation: Dividing a network into separate zones, for example with VLANs, so that a problem in one zone cannot easily spread to the others. A DMZ is a zone for public-facing servers that is separated from the internal network.

8. Least privilege: Giving each user and program only the access it needs and nothing more.

9. Defense in depth: Using several layers of protection, so that if one fails, others still protect the network.

10. Patching: Installing software updates that fix known vulnerabilities.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. Traffic arriving from the internet first meets a firewall, which compares each connection with its rules and blocks anything that is not allowed.

2. Allowed traffic is watched by an IDS or IPS, which compares it with known attack patterns and with normal behavior, and alerts or blocks when something looks wrong.

3. Users and devices must authenticate before they can use the network, and are given only the permissions their role needs.

4. Data that crosses untrusted networks is encrypted, for example by TLS for websites or by a VPN for remote workers.

5. The network is divided into segments, so servers with sensitive data sit in a more protected zone than ordinary user computers.

6. Logs from firewalls, servers and devices are collected and reviewed, often by a security information and event management (SIEM) system, so problems are noticed quickly.

7. Software and device firmware are kept updated, and the network is tested regularly for weaknesses.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
Common attacks on networks:

1. Denial of service (DoS) and distributed denial of service (DDoS): Flooding a server or network with traffic so real users cannot reach it.

2. Man-in-the-middle: An attacker secretly sits between two parties, reading or changing their messages, for example through a fake Wi-Fi hotspot.

3. Packet sniffing: Capturing unencrypted traffic to read passwords or messages.

4. Spoofing: Pretending to be another device or site, such as ARP spoofing on a local network or DNS spoofing.

5. Port scanning: Probing a computer to find open ports and services that might be vulnerable.

6. Brute force and credential stuffing: Trying many passwords, or passwords leaked from other sites, until one works.

7. Phishing: Tricking people into giving up passwords or running malware through fake messages and sites.

8. Malware and ransomware: Harmful programs that spread across a network, and in the case of ransomware, lock files until a payment is made.

Common defenses:

9. Firewalls: packet-filtering, stateful (tracks connections), and next-generation firewalls, plus web application firewalls (WAF) that protect websites.

10. IDS and IPS: network-based or host-based, using signatures of known attacks or detection of unusual behavior.

11. VPNs: remote-access VPNs for individual users and site-to-site VPNs that join two office networks.

12. Endpoint protection, email filtering, and network access control.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
1. A simple firewall rule set. Rules are checked in order, and the last rule blocks everything not allowed above it, which is called default deny:
```
Rule  Action  Source       Destination   Port  Protocol
1     ALLOW   any          web server    443   TCP
2     ALLOW   office net   database      3306  TCP
3     DENY    any          any           any   any
```
Anyone may reach the web server over HTTPS (port 443). Only the office network may reach the database (port 3306). Everything else is blocked.

2. Using public Wi-Fi at a cafe: an attacker on the same network may try to capture traffic. Websites that use HTTPS are encrypted, and a VPN adds encryption for everything the device sends.

3. Multi-factor authentication: even if an attacker learns a password, they also need the code from the user's phone.

4. A DDoS attack: thousands of infected devices send requests to one website at the same time, which overloads it. Defenses include filtering traffic and using services that spread the load across many servers.

5. The Search IT project: user passwords are stored as salted PBKDF2 hashes, so a stolen accounts file does not directly reveal the passwords, and the file is kept out of GitHub with .gitignore. In the online code editor, a forwarded port set to Public can be opened by anyone who has the link, so it should be Private unless it must be shared.

6. A home network checklist: use WPA3 or WPA2 on Wi-Fi with a long password, change the router's default administrator password, update the router firmware, and turn off features you do not use.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Network security protects school and company networks, online banking, hospitals, government systems and home Wi-Fi. Companies use firewalls and VPNs to let employees work remotely, and security teams monitor networks around the clock. Cloud providers and online shops depend on it to protect customer data and to keep their services running.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: Good network security protects private data and the reputation of an organization, keeps services running, and helps meet legal rules about protecting personal information. Layered defense means that one failure does not necessarily lead to a breach, and early detection reduces the damage of an attack.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: No network is completely secure, because new vulnerabilities and attack methods keep appearing, including zero-day flaws that have no fix yet. Security can make systems less convenient, and strict rules may block legitimate work. Encryption protects privacy but also hides attacks from inspection. Insiders and human mistakes, such as falling for phishing, can bypass technical defenses. Detection systems can raise false alarms. Good security costs money, time and trained staff, and it must be maintained continuously.

title: Ethical Hacking
description: An explanation of ethical hacking: authorized, legal testing of systems to find security weaknesses before criminals do, covering permission and scope, the phases of a penetration test, white, gray and black box testing, bug bounty programs, a sample finding report, and the law in the Philippines.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Ethical hacking is the practice of testing a computer system, network or application for security weaknesses with the owner's written permission, in order to fix those weaknesses before criminals can use them. Ethical hackers use many of the same techniques as attackers, but they work legally, follow an agreed plan, keep what they find confidential, and report the problems so they can be repaired. Doing the same actions without permission is a crime. A penetration test, or pen test, is the most common form of ethical hacking.

sections.title: History
sections.content: In the 1970s, the United States government used tiger teams, groups of experts who were asked to break into their own systems to find weaknesses. In 1995, Netscape ran one of the first bug bounty programs, which paid outsiders for reporting flaws in its browser. Google began a bug bounty program in 2010, and platforms such as HackerOne, started in 2012, now connect companies with researchers. The EC-Council launched the Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH) certification in 2003, and other certifications such as CompTIA PenTest+ and OSCP followed. In the Philippines, the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10175) defines illegal access to a computer system as a crime, which is why permission is essential.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Authorization: Written permission from the system's owner before any test begins. Without it, the activity is illegal even if the intention is good.

2. Scope and rules of engagement: The agreed list of what may be tested, what may not, when, and by which methods. Testers must stay inside it.

3. Vulnerability: A weakness that could be used to harm a system, such as an unpatched program or a default password.

4. Exploit: A method or tool that takes advantage of a vulnerability.

5. CVE and CVSS: A CVE is a public ID for a known vulnerability, such as CVE-2021-44228. CVSS is a scoring system from 0.0 to 10.0 that rates how severe a vulnerability is.

6. OWASP Top 10: A widely used list of the most serious security risks for web applications, published by the Open Worldwide Application Security Project.

7. Responsible disclosure: Reporting a vulnerability privately to the owner and giving time to fix it before telling the public.

8. Confidentiality: Findings and any data seen during testing must be protected and shared only with the client.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
A penetration test follows a series of phases:

1. Planning and authorization: The client and tester agree on goals, scope, schedule and rules, and sign a contract and a permission document.

2. Reconnaissance: Collecting information about the target, such as public websites, domain records and technologies in use.

3. Scanning and enumeration: Finding which computers, open ports and services are present, and which versions of software they run.

4. Vulnerability analysis: Comparing what was found with lists of known vulnerabilities and misconfigurations.

5. Controlled exploitation: Carefully confirming that a weakness is real and measuring what it would allow, without causing damage.

6. Impact assessment: Judging how serious the problem is, for example whether it would expose customer data.

7. Reporting: Writing a clear report that describes each finding, its severity, the evidence, and how to fix it.

8. Remediation and retesting: The client repairs the problems, and the tester checks that the fixes work.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
By how much the tester knows:

1. Black box testing: The tester gets no inside information, like an outside attacker.

2. Gray box testing: The tester has limited information, such as a normal user account.

3. White box testing: The tester has full information, such as source code and diagrams.

By target:

4. Network testing, web application testing, wireless testing, mobile app testing, cloud testing, and social engineering tests, which check whether people can be tricked, and physical security tests.

By hat color:

5. White hat: Works legally and with permission, which is the ethical hacker.

6. Black hat: Attacks for personal gain or to cause harm, which is illegal.

7. Gray hat: Tests systems without permission but without harmful intent, which is still illegal in most places.

Team roles: Red teams play attackers, blue teams defend, and purple teams make the two work together. Bug bounty hunters test public programs that invite them and pay for valid reports.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
1. A scope statement: The client allows testing of the school's web server at one named address between 8 PM and 12 AM on a stated weekend, and forbids denial of service tests and access to student records.

2. An entry from a report:
```
Finding:  Default administrator password on router
Severity: High
Evidence: The login page accepted the factory default credentials
Impact:   Someone on the network could change the router settings
Fix:      Set a strong unique password, update the firmware,
          and turn off remote administration
```

3. Checking your own computer. Nmap is a well-known network scanner. Run only against systems you own or have written permission to test. This command lists the open ports and service versions on your own machine:
```
nmap -sV localhost
```

4. Legal places to practice: TryHackMe and Hack The Box offer guided online labs, and OWASP Juice Shop and DVWA are intentionally vulnerable web applications that you can run on your own computer.

5. A bug bounty report: a researcher finds that a website shows another user's data when an ID in the address is changed, reports it privately through the company's program, and receives a reward after it is fixed.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Ethical hacking is used by banks, hospitals, schools, governments and online shops to test their systems before attackers do. Companies hire penetration testers or run bug bounty programs, and many security rules and standards require regular testing. It is also used to test new software and devices before release, and in training, where students practice in safe lab environments.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: It finds real weaknesses before criminals do, which prevents data theft and costly outages. It shows which problems matter most, so limited money and time are spent on the highest risks. It checks whether defenses actually work, tests people as well as technology, and helps an organization meet legal and industry requirements.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: A test shows the situation only at one point in time, and new vulnerabilities appear later. It is limited by its scope and time, so it cannot find everything. Testing can disrupt systems if it is done carelessly. It needs skilled people and can be costly. Most important, it is legal only with permission. Testing a system without authorization can lead to criminal charges, even if the tester means well.

title: Programming Languages Compared
description: A side-by-side comparison of popular programming languages (C, C++, Java, C#, Python, JavaScript, PHP, Kotlin, Swift and Rust) by how they run, how they check types, how they manage memory and what they are mainly used for, with Hello World examples and a guide to choosing one.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A programming language is a formal language used to write instructions that a computer can carry out. There are hundreds of them, and each is designed with different goals, such as speed, safety, simplicity or a specific kind of program. No language is best for everything, so programmers choose one by comparing how it runs, how it handles data types and memory, which libraries it has, and what kind of software they want to build.

sections.title: History
sections.content: FORTRAN, created at IBM by John Backus's team in 1957, was one of the first widely used high-level languages, followed by LISP in 1958 and COBOL in 1959. Dennis Ritchie created C at Bell Labs around 1972. Bjarne Stroustrup began extending C with classes in 1979, and the language was named C++ in 1983. Guido van Rossum released Python in 1991. In 1995, three important languages appeared: Java from Sun Microsystems, led by James Gosling, JavaScript from Brendan Eich at Netscape, and PHP from Rasmus Lerdorf. Microsoft released C# in 2000, designed by a team led by Anders Hejlsberg. Go came from Google in 2009, Rust reached version 1.0 in 2015, Swift was introduced by Apple in 2014, and Kotlin 1.0 was released by JetBrains in 2016, with Google announcing official Kotlin support for Android in 2017.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Compiled language: The whole program is translated by a compiler into machine code before it runs. This usually gives fast programs. Examples: C, C++, Rust.

2. Interpreted language: A program called an interpreter reads and runs the code directly, line by line or in parts, with no separate build step. Example: Python.

3. Bytecode and virtual machine: The compiler translates the code to an intermediate form called bytecode, which a virtual machine runs. The same bytecode runs on any system that has the virtual machine. Examples: Java on the JVM and C# on .NET.

4. Just-in-time (JIT) compilation: The runtime compiles frequently used code to machine code while the program runs. JavaScript engines and the JVM do this.

5. Static typing: The type of each variable is checked before the program runs, so many mistakes are caught early. Examples: Java, C, C++, C#.

6. Dynamic typing: Types are checked while the program runs, which makes code shorter but moves some errors to run time. Examples: Python, JavaScript, PHP.

7. Memory management: In C and C++ the programmer allocates and frees memory manually, which is fast but error-prone. Java, C#, Python and JavaScript use a garbage collector that frees unused memory automatically. Rust uses ownership rules checked at compile time, and Swift uses automatic reference counting.

8. Paradigm: The style of programming a language supports. Procedural (C), object-oriented (Java, C#, C++), functional (parts of JavaScript, Kotlin and Rust) and scripting (Python, PHP).

9. Ecosystem: The libraries, frameworks, tools and community around a language, which often matter as much as the language itself.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
The same idea, source code to running program, happens in different ways:

1. C and C++: A compiler such as gcc turns the source files into a native executable for one type of computer. The executable runs directly on the processor.

2. Java: The compiler javac turns .java files into .class files containing bytecode, and the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) runs them. This is exactly what happens in this project when you run javac -d out *.java and then java -cp out org.example.SearchITWindow.

3. Python: The interpreter reads the .py file, converts it internally to bytecode, and runs it immediately, with no separate compile command.

4. JavaScript: The browser or Node.js engine reads the source, compiles frequently used parts to machine code while the program runs, and executes it.

5. PHP: The PHP engine on a web server runs the script for each request and sends the resulting HTML to the browser.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
A comparison of widely used languages:
```
Language    Typing   Runs as                  Memory             Mainly used for
C           static   native machine code      manual             operating systems, embedded
C++         static   native machine code      manual             games, browsers, performance
Java        static   bytecode on the JVM      garbage collector  enterprise, desktop, Android
C#          static   bytecode on .NET         garbage collector  Windows apps, Unity games
Python      dynamic  interpreted              garbage collector  data science, AI, scripting
JavaScript  dynamic  JIT in browser or Node   garbage collector  websites and web apps
PHP         dynamic  interpreted on server    garbage collector  websites, WordPress
Kotlin      static   bytecode on the JVM      garbage collector  Android apps
Swift       static   native machine code      reference counting iPhone and Mac apps
Rust        static   native machine code      ownership rules    safe systems programming
```

sections.title: Examples
Applications
sections.content: Knowing the strengths of each language helps you choose the right tool for a project, read other people's code, and move to a new language more easily. Many real systems use several languages together. For example, a website may use JavaScript in the browser, Java or Python on the server and SQL in the database, as the Search IT project does with Java, JavaScript and HTML.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: Learning more than one language makes the core ideas clearer, such as variables, loops, functions and objects, because they appear in almost every language. Static typing finds many errors early, dynamic typing makes short programs quick to write, and compiled languages are usually faster. Once you know one language well, a second one takes much less time to learn.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: There is no single best language, and a comparison table simplifies a lot. Performance depends as much on how the code is written as on the language. Popularity changes over time, and rankings such as the TIOBE index and the Stack Overflow Developer Survey measure different things. Fast languages such as C and C++ give more control but make mistakes with memory easier, while easy languages such as Python are slower for heavy calculations. Choosing also depends on the team, the existing code and the available libraries.

title: C++
description: An introduction to C++, a fast compiled language that adds classes, templates and a large standard library to C, covering pointers and manual memory, smart pointers, the Standard Template Library, the build process, worked examples, and how C++ differs from Java.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: C++ is a general-purpose, compiled programming language that supports several styles of programming: procedural, object-oriented and generic. It was created as an extension of C, so most C code also works in C++, and it adds features such as classes, templates and a large standard library. C++ gives the programmer direct control over memory and hardware, which makes it very fast, and it is used where performance matters, such as in games, browsers and system software.

sections.title: History
sections.content: Bjarne Stroustrup began work on the language at Bell Labs in 1979 under the name C with Classes, because he wanted the speed of C together with the classes of Simula. It was renamed C++ in 1983, where the ++ refers to the increment operator of C, and the first commercial release came in 1985. C++ was first standardized by ISO in 1998 and has been updated several times: C++03, then a major modernization in C++11, followed by C++14, C++17, C++20 and C++23. C++11 added features such as auto, lambda expressions, smart pointers and range-based for loops, and C++20 added concepts, ranges, coroutines and modules.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Classes and objects: A class describes a kind of object with data and functions. C++ supports encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism, including multiple inheritance, where a class has more than one parent.

2. Pointers and references: A pointer stores the memory address of a value, and a reference is another name for an existing value. They allow efficient access, but pointers must be handled carefully.

3. Manual memory management: Memory created with new must be released with delete. Forgetting to release it causes a memory leak, and using it after release is a serious bug.

4. RAII and smart pointers: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization ties a resource to the lifetime of an object, so it is released automatically. Smart pointers such as unique_ptr and shared_ptr use this to manage memory safely, and modern C++ prefers them over raw new and delete.

5. Templates: Code that works with any type, written once, such as a vector that can hold integers, text or students. This is called generic programming.

6. Standard Template Library (STL): Ready-made containers such as vector and map, algorithms such as sort and find, and iterators that connect them.

7. Header files and namespaces: Declarations are shared through header files with the #include command, and names such as cout and vector live in the namespace std.

8. Undefined behavior: Some mistakes, such as reading outside an array, have no defined result. The program may crash, give wrong answers, or appear to work, which makes bugs hard to find.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. You write the source code in a .cpp file, and shared declarations in .h or .hpp header files.

2. The preprocessor handles lines that start with #, such as #include, by inserting the contents of the header files.

3. The compiler translates each .cpp file into an object file of machine code.

4. The linker joins the object files and libraries into one executable file.

5. The operating system runs the executable directly on the processor, with no virtual machine. This is why C++ programs are fast.

Common compilers are GCC (g++), Clang and Microsoft Visual C++. A typical command with GCC is:
```
g++ -std=c++17 hello.cpp -o hello
./hello
```

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
C++ standards (each adds new features):

1. C++98 and C++03: The first ISO standard and a small fix.

2. C++11: Modern C++ begins, with auto, lambdas, smart pointers and move semantics.

3. C++14 and C++17: Smaller improvements, such as simpler generic code and filesystem support.

4. C++20 and C++23: Concepts, ranges, coroutines, modules and more library features.

Programming styles supported:

5. Procedural, object-oriented, generic (templates), and functional ideas such as lambdas.

sections.title: Examples
Applications
sections.content: C++ is used for game engines such as Unreal Engine, for web browsers such as Chrome and Firefox, for databases such as MongoDB, and for much of the Adobe software and desktop applications. It is used in trading systems that must respond in microseconds, in embedded systems and robotics, in simulations, and in parts of operating systems and virtual reality software.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: C++ programs are very fast and use memory efficiently, and the programmer can control exactly how hardware and memory are used. It supports several styles of programming and has a mature, standardized language with huge libraries. Code can be compiled for almost any platform, and it can work directly with existing C libraries.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: C++ is large and complex, so it takes a long time to learn well. Manual memory handling makes errors such as leaks, dangling pointers and buffer overflows possible, and these are a common cause of security problems. Undefined behavior makes some bugs hard to find. Compile times can be long, error messages from templates are difficult to read, and programs must be compiled separately for each operating system. For these reasons, newer languages such as Rust and safer parts of modern C++ aim to reduce memory errors.

title: PHP
description: An introduction to PHP, the server-side scripting language behind many websites, covering how a PHP page is processed by the web server, variables and forms, connecting to a database safely with prepared statements, frameworks and WordPress, and common security mistakes.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: PHP is a server-side scripting language designed for building websites and web applications. A PHP script runs on the web server, not in the visitor's browser. It can read form data, talk to a database, and create the HTML page that is sent back. The visitor only receives the finished HTML, never the PHP code. The name PHP is a recursive acronym that stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.

sections.title: History
sections.content: Rasmus Lerdorf created the first version in 1994 as a set of tools for his personal home page, which is where the original name Personal Home Page came from, and released it publicly in 1995. In 1998, Zeev Suraski and Andi Gutmans rewrote the engine for PHP 3, and the language was renamed PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor. PHP 4 introduced the Zend Engine in 2000, and PHP 5 in 2004 greatly improved object-oriented programming. PHP 7, released in December 2015, made scripts much faster, and PHP 8, released in November 2020, added a just-in-time compiler, named arguments, union types and the match expression. New versions are released every year, in November. Popular PHP projects include WordPress, Wikipedia's MediaWiki software, and the Laravel framework, first released in 2011.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. Server-side execution: The code runs on the web server and produces HTML, so the browser never sees the PHP source.

2. PHP tags: PHP code is placed between the tags that open with a less-than sign, a question mark and the letters php, and close with a question mark and a greater-than sign. Everything outside these tags is sent as plain HTML.

3. Variables: Names that start with a dollar sign, such as $name. PHP is dynamically typed, and newer versions allow optional type declarations.

4. Superglobals: Built-in arrays that are always available, such as $_GET for data in the address, $_POST for submitted form data, $_SESSION for data kept between pages, and $_COOKIE.

5. Sessions and cookies: Ways to remember a user between page requests, for example to keep someone logged in.

6. Database access: PHP connects to databases such as MySQL through PDO or MySQLi. Prepared statements keep user input separate from the SQL command.

7. Composer: PHP's package manager, which downloads and updates libraries for a project.

8. Shared-nothing request model: Each request starts a fresh run of the script, and nothing is kept in memory afterward unless it is stored in a session, a database or a cache.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. A visitor's browser requests a page such as search.php from the web server, for example Apache or Nginx.

2. The web server sees that the file is PHP and passes it to the PHP interpreter.

3. PHP runs the script from top to bottom. It may read form data, check a session, and query a database.

4. The output of the script, usually HTML, replaces the PHP code.

5. The web server sends the finished HTML to the browser, which displays it.

6. The script ends, and its memory is released. The next request starts again from the beginning.

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
Ways PHP is used:

1. Dynamic web pages: Scripts embedded in or generating HTML. This is the main use.

2. Content management systems (CMS): WordPress, Drupal and Joomla are written in PHP.

3. Web frameworks: Laravel and Symfony give structure for larger applications, including routing, database tools and security features.

4. Command-line scripts: PHP can run tasks from the terminal, such as scheduled jobs.

5. Web APIs: PHP programs can return JSON to mobile apps and JavaScript front ends.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content: 1. A page that mixes PHP with HTML: ``` Hello, ' . $name . '!'; ?> ``` The browser receives only the heading Hello, Ana! 2. Reading a search word from the address. Opening search.php?q=java shows the text You searched for: java: ``` ``` The function htmlspecialchars converts special characters so that a visitor cannot inject a script into the page. 3. A safe database query with a prepared statement. The question mark is filled in by the database driver, so the input cannot change the SQL command: ``` $pdo = new PDO('mysql:host=localhost;dbname=school', 'user', 'pass'); $stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT name FROM students WHERE course = ?'); $stmt->execute(['BSIT']); $rows = $stmt->fetchAll(); ``` 4. Trying PHP on your own computer with its built-in test server: ``` php -S localhost:8000 ``` Then open http://localhost:8000 in the browser. This is for learning only and is not for a real website. 5. Compared with the Search IT project: the Java server answers a request to /api/search with JSON, and the same job in PHP would be a script that reads $_GET['q'], searches the data, and prints JSON.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: PHP runs a large share of the websites on the internet, mostly because it powers WordPress, which is used for blogs, company sites and online shops. It is used for e-commerce platforms such as WooCommerce and Magento, for forums, for the MediaWiki software behind Wikipedia, and for custom business applications built with Laravel. Facebook was originally written in PHP, and Slack and Etsy also used it.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: PHP is easy to start with, and almost every web hosting company supports it, often at low cost. It was built for the web, so common tasks such as handling forms, sessions and cookies are simple. It has good documentation, a very large community, and ready-made systems like WordPress. Since PHP 7, performance is much better, and modern PHP supports classes, types and tools such as Composer.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Older PHP code often has inconsistent function names and poor structure, and it is easy to write messy code. Careless code is open to serious security problems, such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and unsafe file uploads, so input must always be validated and database queries should use prepared statements. Because each request starts fresh, PHP is less natural for long-running or real-time applications, although tools exist for that. Many new projects choose other technologies such as Node.js, Python or Java.

title: C# (C Sharp)
description: An introduction to C# (pronounced C sharp), Microsoft's object-oriented language that runs on the .NET platform, covering classes and properties, how code is compiled to intermediate language and run by the CLR, LINQ, async and await, a comparison with Java, and what it is used for, including Unity games.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: C# (pronounced C sharp) is a modern, statically typed, object-oriented programming language created by Microsoft. C# programs run on .NET, a software platform that provides a runtime, a large class library and tools. The language is used to build desktop apps, websites and web services, cloud services, mobile apps and games. Its syntax is similar to Java and C++, so programmers who know one of them can learn it quickly.

sections.title: History
sections.content: C# was designed at Microsoft by a team led by Anders Hejlsberg, who had earlier created Turbo Pascal and Delphi. It was announced in 2000 as part of Microsoft's .NET initiative, and the first version of the .NET Framework was released in 2002. C# was standardized by Ecma International (ECMA-334) in 2002 and by ISO in 2003. Important additions over the years include generics in C# 2.0 (2005), LINQ in C# 3.0 (2007), and async and await in C# 5.0 (2012). In 2016, Microsoft released .NET Core, an open-source version that runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, and in 2020 it was combined with the other .NET versions under the name .NET 5. A new version of .NET and C# is released every year in November.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
1. .NET and the CLR: The Common Language Runtime (CLR) is the engine that runs C# programs, manages memory and handles errors. The .NET class library supplies ready-made code for files, networking, data and more.

2. Intermediate Language (IL): The C# compiler turns source code into IL, a form similar to Java bytecode. The CLR then compiles IL to machine code just in time while the program runs.

3. Classes and objects: C# is fully object-oriented, with encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. A class can inherit from only one class but can implement many interfaces.

4. Properties: A shorter way to write getters and setters. A property looks like a field but can run code when it is read or changed.

5. Value types and reference types: A struct is a value type that is copied when assigned, and a class is a reference type that is shared through a reference.

6. Generics: Code that works with any type, such as a list of integers or a list of students, while still being type-checked.

7. LINQ (Language Integrated Query): Query syntax built into the language for filtering, sorting and grouping collections, arrays, databases and XML.

8. Delegates, events and lambdas: Ways to pass methods around and react to events, such as a button click.

9. async and await: A simple way to write code that waits for slow work, such as a network request, without freezing the program.

10. Garbage collection and NuGet: Memory is freed automatically, and NuGet is the package manager for libraries.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
1. You write source code in .cs files, using an editor such as Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code.

2. The C# compiler checks the types and translates the code into IL, stored in an assembly, which is a .dll or .exe file.

3. When the program starts, the CLR loads the assembly.

4. The just-in-time compiler converts the IL into machine code for the current computer, and the program runs.

5. The garbage collector frees memory that is no longer used.

With the .NET command-line tool, the steps for a new console program are:
```
dotnet new console -o Hello
cd Hello
dotnet run
```

sections.title: Types
sections.content:
Kinds of programs built with C#:

1. Desktop apps: Windows Forms and WPF for Windows, and cross-platform interfaces such as .NET MAUI and Avalonia.

2. Web applications and APIs: ASP.NET Core, which runs on Windows, Linux and macOS.

3. Games: The Unity game engine uses C# as its scripting language.

4. Cloud and enterprise services: Widely used with Microsoft Azure.

5. Mobile apps: .NET MAUI and its predecessor Xamarin.

6. Console tools and background services.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
1. A complete program, using a feature called top-level statements:
```
Console.WriteLine("Hello, World!");
```

2. A class with properties:
```
public class Student
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public int Grade { get; set; }
}
```
The properties replace the separate getName and setName methods that Java would need.

3. LINQ to filter a list:
```
var scores = new List<int> { 90, 85, 77 };
var high = scores.Where(s => s >= 80).ToList();
Console.WriteLine(high.Count);
```
The output is 2, because only 90 and 85 are at least 80.

4. C# compared with Java, the language of this course:
```
Feature            C#                              Java
Runs on            CLR (.NET)                      JVM
Compiled to        IL                              bytecode
Getters/setters    properties                      methods
Value types        struct                          primitives only
Query collections  LINQ                            streams
Owner              Microsoft                       Oracle
```
The two languages are very similar, so knowing Java makes C# easy to learn.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: C# is used for Windows desktop software, web services built with ASP.NET Core, and business systems in banks and large companies. It is the main language for Unity, one of the most widely used game engines, which makes it popular for mobile and indie games. It is also used heavily on Microsoft Azure for cloud services.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.content: C# is a clean, modern language with strong tooling, especially in Visual Studio. Static typing finds many mistakes before the program runs, and features such as properties, LINQ and async and await make code short and readable. With .NET, programs run on Windows, Linux and macOS, and a large library and a large community support it. Performance is good, and it is well suited to large projects.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: The language is closely connected to Microsoft's ecosystem, and some tools and frameworks work best on Windows. The .NET platform is large, and its many versions and frameworks, such as the older .NET Framework and the newer .NET, can be confusing at first. Programs need the .NET runtime to run unless they are packaged together with it. Memory use is higher than in C or C++, and the garbage collector can cause short pauses. Fewer open-source libraries exist than for some other languages.
